Research|AIDC: Texas Permitting Risks Rise After Midterm Elections; 2027 Delivery Forecast Unchanged

In the November 3 midterm elections, Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. Texas was the biggest surprise: Talarico won the U.S. Senate seat, becoming the first Democrat to win the seat since 1988. Hinojosa defeated Abbott, who was seeking a fourth term, while several statewide offices, including lieutenant governor, attorney general and comptroller, also changed hands. Republicans are still expected to control the Texas Senate. The final composition of the Texas House and the comptroller race should be updated before publication based on the certified vote count.

Data centers were one of the central issues in the election. Hinojosa pledged to impose a moratorium on new data centers until the legislature establishes safeguards; require projects to demonstrate that they will not raise residential electricity or water bills; prohibit developers from signing NDAs with local governments; and eliminate the sales tax exemption for data centers (6.25%, for up to 20 years, with an estimated two-year fiscal cost of approximately $3.2bn). The freeze was already underway. On August 3, Abbott halted the ERCOT large-load queue (approximately 474GW of applications, around 90% of which were data centers, or more than five times Texas’ historical peak load) and ordered a project-by-project review. ERCOT subsequently delayed Batch Zero in its new interconnection process. On September 21, Abbott also directed TCEQ not to issue any data-center-related permits until the ERCOT and TWDB audits are complete, with all state agencies suspending related approvals. The ERCOT audit is expected in early December, but its completion will not automatically restart permitting.

Before the election, the market broadly expected Abbott to win re-election and was focused on when the freeze would be lifted after the audits were completed. Hinojosa’s victory could mean a longer freeze and tighter conditions for reopening the permitting process. However, she said during the campaign that she was not opposed to data centers. Her proposals focused mainly on protecting household utility bills and giving communities a say in site selection. The main impact of the election, therefore, is likely to be on how long the freeze remains in place and the conditions under which permitting resumes. Under our base case, we are temporarily maintaining our 2027 delivery forecast. Supporting that view will require a closer review of project permitting status: how much capacity has obtained key permits, how much Texas capacity remains subject to approval, and how much delay is already reflected in the original model. If the freeze lasts longer than assumed in the base case, or the probability of the downside scenario increases, expected deliveries could also be revised lower. New projects in Texas face greater exposure in 2028: most are likely to be delayed, while some demand may shift to other states.

quoted.text:
Tell your agent to optimize your site’s web fonts. I’m seeing a huge difference on my blog.

Full prompt:

Make this site's web fonts load faster without changing how anything looks. Shrink font bytes as far as possible, keep rendering identical, and prove it with before/after pixel diffs. Treat any visual change as a regression unless I approve it. If an optimization would change rendering, tell me what it saves and what it changes, and keep the site looking the same by default. Keep the current loading behavior: don't touch font-display or fallback fonts. Don't add font processing to the build; write a script I run by hand, commit its output, and note when it needs rerunning. First measure the current state: each font file's size, glyph count, variable axes, OpenType features and hinting, plus font bytes per page and what each page preloads. Then find out what the site actually uses, checking inline component styles as well as stylesheets: which characters appear in the content, which axis values and weights each font needs (including one-off overrides and bold inside italics), which OpenType features are turned on, and CSS side effects like `hyphens: auto` using the U+2010 hyphen. Cut each font down to that. Keep the used characters plus Latin-1 and Latin Extended-A, and leave CJK to system fonts if that's how it renders today. Limit variable axes to the ranges in use, and only fix an axis at one value if nothing overrides it. Drop unused OpenType features and hinting. Split each font into two files. A small core with ASCII and the punctuation most pages use (curly quotes, dashes, ellipsis) gets preloaded. An extended file behind `unicode-range` only downloads when a page needs one of its characters. Each file's `unicode-range` should list only characters it actually contains. Watch out for a few things. A generated fallback face between the core and extended files will draw the extended characters before the real font does. Fonts with a Reserved Font Name under the OFL must be renamed internally once subset. Check the generated files, since font tools have quirks. Before calling it done, build a baseline from the same content and pixel-diff before and after on pages with code, italics, accented characters, components with their own font settings, and CJK. Explain every visible difference: content change, regression to fix, or harmless sub-pixel rounding. Re-measure bytes per page and confirm the extended files only load where needed. When you're done, tell me the bytes before and after per font and per page, the pixel-diff results, anywhere you deviated from what I asked and what it cost, and how to rerun the script. Later, it may be worth embedding the core font in the global stylesheet and precaching the extended files after idle.

quoted.text:
We need to reconsider our priors on code readability.

Humans, compared to agents, are pretty slow at understanding large quantities of text. So in the old days, readability was important so the human could efficiently grok what was going on.

So readability now comes down to:

1. Can a human, if needed, jump in and understand the code
2. Does the code use the same domain language as the human describing the code?

1 helps with observability and the occasional spot checks you need to do on important PR's. 2 helps the agent translate the words you use into code changes.

In other words, readability is now a nicety, not a necessity.

The way agents 'read' code is different - good agents are all about gathering data about how the code works. They'll prod around with it, execute parts of it.

So 'readability' to agents really means 'verifiability'. How easy it is to mess about with that code to see it working.

Let's take this scenario:

- You have a huge module in your codebase that uses all sorts of complex performance tricks
- It has 100% test coverage

A talented human would need an hour or two to get comfortable working in that module.

An agent needs zero time. They verify it with the tests, poke about a bit, and they're good to go.

The takeaways:

- When judging a module (or a codebase), don't think about how easy the code is to read
- Instead, think about how easy it is to verify
- Design your codebase so modules can be tested and verified independently
- Feel free to sacrifice a bit of readability for performance
- Cyclomatic complexity and function size don't matter to agents

quoted.text:
Rust 的编译速度和构建产物占用，已成为 AI 时代的严重瓶颈。

多个 agents 并行、多 worktree，反复 build 和 check，再强的 CPU 也经常被打满，一个个几十 G 起步的 target 一点一点吃掉磁盘空间（并且今年 SSD 还那么贵）。

AI 写代码越来越快，构建成本越来越显眼。

如果有一门能有 Go 一样的编译速度，又有 Rust 那样无 GC、内存安全，以及深入底层做极致性能优化的能力，那将是最适合 AI 时代的编程语言。

An update on building games with Claude Code:

Last week some of you ran into Claude Code pushing back on game projects it should have just built. We'd added a short rule to the Opus 5.5 prompt to steer Claude away from recreating specific existing games, but it was also kicking in when you referenced one just to describe the mechanics you wanted.

We've updated that rule in 2.1.317. You can name a game to describe what you want and Claude should now build an original game in that genre. If you ask for a copy of the original, it'll offer to build something similar instead.

We want Claude to be as helpful as possible when you're building something original, but also to protect your work if someone else tries to copy it. We'll keep improving this, so let us know if Claude turns down work that's yours. Thanks to everyone who shared feedback!

text:
This is my superagent

A recipe for a fleet-conductor skill, in 10 points:

1. **One brain, many hands.** Conductor routes, gates, decides. Never edits code itself. Workers = long-lived themed lanes (own worktree, own agent); reuse a free lane before spawning a new one. Budget per host: N sandboxes, M orchestrators; check RAM/load before starting anything.

2. **Engine on an always-on host, cockpit on the laptop.** Fleet + state daemon run on the server. Laptop = driver for things that need the human: authed browser, prod-write keys, headed reviews. Jobs queue in a mailbox until the laptop pulls them; nothing blocks on a sleeping laptop.

3. **Structured bus, not chatter.** Workers report one line with a state (progress/ready/blocked/ask). A daemon turns screens + reports into stages (answer/blocked/prompt/review/working/idle) and logs only changes. The conductor watches one event stream. No acks, no status noise.

4. **Self-healing host.** A global lock for heavy jobs (re-entrant), concurrency caps, OOM policy that doesn't take down every lane, auto-updates off, a watchdog that revives killed sessions with `--continue`. Silent death is the worst failure; detect it.

5. **Integration-branch mode by default.** Parallel lanes = local branches, no per-lane PRs or pushes. Local AI review (codex/claude) per branch, lead merges in batches (rerere, one owner per hot file), one local check, one PR → one hosted CI + bot review. Smuggle small fixes into in-flight work; roll up instead of fanning out.

6. **Gates = evidence, not vibes.** Each merge needs: a review that actually ran (check its output, not its exit code), runtime proof in a sandbox, a rule audit by a cheap model, and before/after for customer-visible changes. Never call an unrun check a pass.

7. **Refactors need a feature inventory.** Before a big rewrite, crawl the old code into a feature tree (screens, actions, rules, jobs, emails). Every node is CARRIED/FOLDED/SIMPLIFIED/ALLOWED-REMOVAL/MISSING, with proof. A removal needs a register row the human signs. Diff the outputs (reports, totals) old vs new.

8. **Human owns one-way doors.** Prod SQL, deploys, secrets, money writes, outbound messages, risky merges → human, with the exact text or command shown. Everything reversible: decide, act, inform. Ask one question at a time, with a recommended answer, in a decision panel, not a wall of text.

9. **Least privilege per tier.** Sandboxes get test keys only. Read-only prod keys live in one private file on the server, never in worktrees. Prod writes happen only from the driver with the human present. IDs only (no PII) in PRs, issues and notes. Never print secrets.

10. **Learning loop.** Every user correction becomes a durable rule (skill text, worker brief, memory) the same turn, synced to every host. Post-launch items go to one tracked list (a gist). The skill stays the source of truth; briefs inherit from it.

Garry Tan reveals why Y Combinator decides in just 10 minutes whether or not to fund a founder

"The wild thing about Y Combinator is that we get 80,000, maybe 90,000 applications a year now for about 800 spots. So it is less than a 1% acceptance rate. Maybe 8 to 10% of those people would get an interview, sometimes less now."

"And the wild thing is we actually spend only 10 minutes with them for that final stage."

"Paul Graham, the founder of YC, figured out that you didn't need half an hour, you don't need an hour. And then you could probably actually do it in about 5 minutes, but 5 minutes feels rude. So that's how YC ended up at 10 minutes."

"It sounds almost too simple, but 10 minutes is a wonderful constraint. Like how 140 characters for Twitter way back in the day was a wonderful constraint. If you can say something very simply that hits us, here's a user, here's a real person who has a problem, and here's how the technology that we build actually solves that. We just want to know what it is and why it's awesome."

"And then if we have a little bit of extra time, we want to know why that founder is the person to go and build that thing. And you can do all of that in 10 minutes. And it's an up-down decision."

"Something like 10% to 15% of all self-made billionaires as of now, aged 50 and under, are YC alums."

Walter Isaacson: "Let's say Elon Musk, he walked in and you had 10 minutes with him. What do you think the percentage chance is that you would actually fund him?"

Garry Tan: "100%. In current form, 100%. I had a managing partner meeting the other day, and that's actually one of the example questions we ask ourselves to figure out whether we're on the right track."

"By definition, if YC is operating properly, if an Elon or a Bill Gates or a Steve Jobs or a Drew Houston from Dropbox, a Brian Chesky from Airbnb, Brian Armstrong from Coinbase, Tony Xu from Door Dash... if someone like that walks into our office, can we say yes to them in 10 minutes? And if that answer is no, actually I'd have to rewrite everything. We'd have to retool everything. That is almost the only question that really matters when it comes to whether YC is doing well or not."

libghostty has always been fast, but it's also been getting significantly faster. Here are IO throughput measurements comparing Ghostty 1.3.1, 1.4.0, and main as of this morning. We'll be backporting most of these to a 1.4.1 release soon.

Here are some highlights of the changes since 1.4:

- Ghostty 1.4 had a fast-path for printing runs of plain text. But the fast-path only applied to limited cases. We now support mixed width characters and hyperlinks in the fast path.

- Our input path always widened the pty data to codepoints (8-bit to 32-bit) as part of UTF-8 decode, which also incurred a memory copy. We now have a SIMD fast path to detect pure-ASCII and we process the run direct from the read buffer (no copy, narrower data).

- New memory pages use most recent two pages actual utilization to pre-size themselves accordingly. This sped up styles, hyperlinks etc.

- When a VM page runs out of capacity for a certain type of data (e.g. hyperlinks, styles), we now project the usage so far to guess what you'll need, then shrink available rows to avoid a realloc. Before we'd naively double. This caused a classic "laddering" problem.

- We recognized "erase" being a slow path for us, and it's a common sequence, so we use another bit in row headers to track blank (we had space).

- Styles are now processed once per SGR. Previously, a sequence like "ESC[1;38;2;r;g;bm" would apply each style as it came in (1, then 38, then 2, etc.). We now apply all attributes at once and write to the cursor atomically.

- Styles are now packed into 128-bit values and use aarch64 and x86_64-specific assembly for minimizing instructions to use it.

- On x86_64, we found that LLVM was lowering some row resets (hot path) to a 4-byte store followed by an 8-byte load which couldn't be store-forwarded. This caused an almost 10% (!!!) slowdown on scroll operations only on x86_64. The fix was to change our reset to build the full header in a register then do a single memmove per row.

Net results are what you see in the graph, but written out main to 1.4: ASCII 1.5x, heavy styling 1.5x, styled Unicode 1.8x, random UTF-8 1.4x, random OSC 8 2.7x, mixed styled text with links 4.8x, cursor/erase 16x, hyperlink-dense text 5.6x.

any sm/med company who is AI-pilled is starting to rebuild their whole GTM-stack and old tools are not making the cut

larger companies are slower to react due to long contracts and tough change management, but as agent-native tools mature, the cost and effort of switching will drop dramatically for them as well

some changes that i'm seeing:

Websites: Webflow/Framer struggled to make their tools more AI-native. Companies transfer to a headless local setup + @sanity_io  or use tools like @ployai  (Agentic websites). We churned Webflow at the beginning of this year - now it's so easy to run PLG experiments, programmatic SEO pages, agent-powered experiments... The speed + lvl of control is insane.. and everyone on the team is shipping code

Enrichment: Clay has been on red alert since January (although to their credit, they've adapted to AI faster than anyone else on this list). The first hit came from claude code, now it's native agent tools like @firecrawl  that will eat their lunch (same waterfall system, enough data source, and obviously a lot more cheaper). Clay created the GTM engineer, but that same person is now getting more AI-pilled and has the lowest switching cost. Also their agency channel is being disrupted as well, these people are always on the lookout to optimize their processes and cut on costs

Workflows: N8N/Gumloop are still being used, but some teams just rely on good skills.md files in their personal agents or coding agents for various tasks and it's pretty reliable. Most interestingly also, is the rise of agent harnesses where you can just say "get 30% more sales this month" and let the agent figure out how (@hone is building something amazing here)

SEO/GEO : Tools like @openseo gain popularity (and thank god because Ahrefs has been awful lately), but every bit of written content on your website now is meant for an agent more than a human. So, many companies are optimizing their written content for GEO, and creating a lot of assets like benchmarks or other social proof so that agents can build more confidence and recommend your tool. @gauge_sh is one tool I've really liked using (team is amazing too!), although I think GEO strategy matters far more than the tool right now (most of them do the same thing e.g. Airops/Profound).

CRM: Most companies are locked into their existing pre-AI era CRM, and they're trying to query data with coding agents. That works amazingly well (esp compared to pre-AI), but there are a lot of companies who'll try to build a more native AI-CRM and i'm excited to see how that will play out. There are lots of YC companies trying to disrupt this, one that I've seen is @lightfld

growth is becoming an engineering problem, and eng is being disrupted by AI so you do the math here - it's going to be an intense winter season for old SaaS

quoted.text:
Seeing this makes the end-state clearer to me: code that can't be read by humans, run on machines that humans can't access, via inaccessible APIs, trained on data that humans didn't create.

LLMs are starting to get really good at manipulating mostly-opaque-to-humans code (see: their improved ability to reverse engineer machine code/assembly). Additionally, folks are accessing more-and-more of their LLMs in cloud-based environments without ever actually interacting with an LLM API (myself included).

I think it's going to become increasingly likely that the end state is one in which you ask an agentic company to produce some result and it does it via [some system completely opaque to humans] and produces [some output in a format that humans are unable to interpret].

It makes me wonder if our current state of competing LLMs cross-training on each other will eventually become literally impossible (not just logistically so) when they become fully self-recursive and are producing output that even other LLMs can't understand, let alone humans.

I think we're in something of a golden period here where humans are still capable of understanding how things work and how things are run (shell commands! python! node.js!) but it's going to quickly become irrelevant. We're already past the previous high-point where we were able to see reasoning traces for the top-level LLMs.

I'm skeptical that open models will ever get to this point as the economics are working against them (I suspect that they will always need human-generated training materials in one form or another). But it does make me wonder if the upper-echelon companies will end up converging into this high-level "black box that produces outputs" singularity of sorts.

This has been hitting home for me lately as I've been using Claude Projects in a cloud-based environment where I can't see transcripts, look at the machine it's running on, nor even know what commands it's running. I don't even know what languages its writing its code in. We're just a couple steps away from code being completely irrelevant.

Humans are ~1,000,000x more sample efficient than LLMs, and there are no good explanations.

We’ve found that a big part of the answer is that LLMs are *massively* underparameterized by many orders of magnitude. The brain has 100T synapses learning from ~200M tokens of language. Chinchilla prescribes a 1T-parameter model on 20T tokens. That’s 7 OOMs apart in parameters per token.

After a lot of painstaking work, we present new data-constrained scaling laws and learning algorithms to scale to (extrapolated) quadrillion-parameter transformers.

quoted.text:
10 Spicy Takes After Talking to 50 Friends at the Frontier of Robotics 🤖🔥

1/ Astra IS robotics' GPT-3 moment. Ironically, now that it's finally here, some in robotics seem reluctant to acknowledge it. Perhaps because it (sadly) didn't come from a robotics company?

2/ Robotics is becoming just another vertical for frontier labs. Not so different from coding in some respects. Why reinvent general intelligence for every industry?

3/ Robotics was too hard to underwrite until now. No convincing pretraining scaling law, no convergence on models, data, or hardware. No wonder some critics dismissed it as a fragmented industry playing an expensive "demo game". Astra may finally offer a credible path to scale.

4/ Robotics foundation-model startups have a case. But how strong is it? The argument: Astra handles System 2 (reasoning), while specialized models retain System 1 (skills) and System 0 (motor control). Fair. But isn't that already a narrower value proposition? And who says the boundary stops there?

5/ Follow the talent. Word is OpenAI reorganized its 30–40-person robotics team around the core Astra model. Hearing similar moves toward general models at @Tesla_Optimus. Org charts may tell us more than any demo.

6/ The robotics data gold rush is real. Million-hour procurement programs, some potentially reaching tens of millions of hours. Talk of budgets approaching $1B per frontier lab.

7/ Bullish on robotics hardware volumes. As intelligence becomes more accessible, the barriers to building useful robots could fall dramatically. The moat shifts toward reliability, dexterity, integration, and deployment.

8/ Robotics could fuel the next semiconductor and memory supercycle. A 100B-parameter model running on the edge requires ~50GB just for 4-bit weights. Now multiply that by millions of robots. Why do you think @JensenHuang is so obsessed with robotics? @elonmusk saw it coming: https://t.co/oKQi0XDhiL

9/ Is self-driving immune to the general-model threat? After coding and robotics, why assume self-driving remains the exclusive domain of proprietary, vertical models? Robotaxi increasingly feels like a solved problem to me. But if and when frontier labs move into self-driving, we could see an Apple vs. Android dynamic. Think about the implications for $TSLA, Waymo, and other OEMs.

10/ The next bottleneck may not be intelligence. It's deployment. Models are improving faster than our ability to deploy robots in the messy real world. Integration, hardware variance, failure recovery, and economics remain brutally hard. The real moat may be turning intelligence into reliable, profitable physical work.

--
I realize some of these takes may rub people the wrong way, especially those who have spent years doing the hard work of advancing robotics. That's not my intention.

I'm sharing them to spark debate, not to declare winners and losers. Astra has only been out for a month or so, and it's far too early to draw definitive conclusions. More importantly, when the TAM is this enormous - potentially the largest in tech - there should be plenty of room for different approaches and many winners.

++

start with /poteto-mode to route the task through the right playbook

> Define the task

launch → doctor → drive → evidence → cleanup

The proof depends on the change:

→ UI: complete the affected user journey
→ CLI: capture the command, output and exit status
→ storage: read back the written value
→ performance: compare profiles under equivalent conditions

> Hand off the tested change

tested_commit / diff / commands + results / evidence_paths

Failed checks send the change back for repair

Unavailable checks stay listed under unverified_checks, with the missing dependency explained

> Prevent recurring failures

/reflect - captures the lesson

/correct - helps encode it through architecture, types, lint, CI or tests

作为一个一直只写 Next.js 的人，我为什么也开始被 TanStack Start 圈粉了？ 老实讲，在这之前我一直是个纯正的 Next.js 肌肉记忆患者。

每次开新项目，不管是做学习平台 LearnX 还是写各种小工具，我的第一反应永远是无脑跑 create-next-app。对于最近半年在外网独立开发者圈子里火得一塌糊涂的 TanStack Start，我之前其实一直没真正上手用过，心里甚至觉得：「Next.js 生态这么稳，干嘛还要去折腾一个新框架？」

直到最近我在打磨自己的全栈底座 Supastack 时，发现身边越来越多硬核开发者（尤其是重度使用 Cursor 和 Claude Code 的朋友）都在念叨 TanStack。出于好奇，我们专门去深扒了一下它的架构逻辑，甚至直接把 TanStack Start 作为第二套 Web 引擎（apps/web-tanstack）完整接进了我们的底座仓库里。

看完这套用 TanStack 搭出来的代码结构后，我终于明白为什么那么多老程序员对它上头了。如果用最直白的话总结它的好，核心就三点：

1. 没有「黑盒魔法」，它对 AI 写代码太友好了我们平时用 Next.js App Router 配合 AI 写代码时，最头疼的往往不是写业务逻辑，而是跟框架的「隐式规则」打架： 这个文件到底在服务端跑还是客户端跑？为什么加了一行代码就报 Hydration 水合错误？为什么数据库明明改了，页面却被某层看不见的缓存卡住了？哪怕你给 AI 写了一大堆 Prompt 规则，它还是经常在 'use client' 和 Server Actions 的边界上发疯。

而 TanStack Start 的设计哲学刚好反过来：极致的显式（Explicit）。

它不搞那些靠隐式指令和暗箱缓存自动触发的黑魔法，哪怕同样是文件路由，每个路由也都是通过 createFileRoute 显式声明，所有边界和逻辑都是清清楚楚的 TypeScript 函数：

路由加载前要验权或拉数据？直接写在明面上的 beforeLoad 和 loader 里；
要调服务端接口读写数据？直接用 createServerFn 定义，配合 .validator() 校验，输入输出全带严格类型。

这种设计在 AI 时代有一个巨大的红利：因为没有任何隐藏在框架背后的潜规则，AI 读代码上下文的时候一眼就能看懂数据是怎么流的，写出来的代码准确率高得离谱，几乎不会出现精神分裂式的幻觉。

2. 把路由和 URL 参数做成了 100% 的「类型安全」以前写复杂的后台页面，最容易出低级 Bug 的地方就是改路由名字和传 URL 参数（比如 ?page=2&filter=paid）。很多时候你改了一个页面的路径，或者改了一个参数名，编译器根本不会报错，只有等用户点进去变成了 404 或者页面崩了你才知道。

TanStack Router 最绝的地方，就是把 端到端类型安全（End-to-End Type Safety） 塞进了每一个链接里。 不管是自动生成的路由树路径、动态参数，还是通过 validateSearch 声明的 URL 查询条件，全都是强类型的。只要你改了一个路由结构或参数定义，不用打开浏览器点测试，编辑器里的 tsc 会在一秒钟内把全站所有没对齐的跳转链接全部标红。对强迫症和独立开发者来说，这种安全感真的很难拒绝。

3. 轻快、纯粹，不绑架你的底层业务除了底层基于 Vite 带来的毫秒级热更新速度之外，这次把 TanStack Start 塞进 Supastack 的过程，也让我彻底跑通了一个很爽的架构思路：

其实我们根本不需要在 Next.js 和 TanStack 之间痛苦地二选一。

在设计 Supastack 的时候，我们把 90% 最耗时、最容易踩坑的核心商业基建——包括 Drizzle 数据库 Schema、鉴权逻辑、Stripe/Creem/Polar 等 8 家出海支付的幂等账本、AI 路由、邮件系统、20 多套主题以及跨框架复用的页面核心（web-core）——全部抽离到了底层的共享 packages/* 里。

在这个共享底座之上，我们同时配好了 apps/web 和 apps/web-tanstack 两套现成的 Web 引擎：

如果你像以前的我一样习惯了 Next.js 16，或者强依赖它的生态，直接开箱就用；
如果你想尝试 TanStack Start 极致的类型安全和干净的显式代码，不用自己从头配环境、不用重新写一遍登录和支付，直接切过去就能跑同一套完整的商业闭环（甚至还能同步复用仓库里的 Expo 移动端和 Tauri 桌面端）。

如果你之前也像我一样只听说过 TanStack 的大名、还没来得及自己配环境试水，或者想看看同一套全栈业务在 Next.js 和 TanStack 下分别长什么样，可以直接去我们的文档和在线演示里看现成的实现：

Lightberry wants to charge $20,000 a year for software running on a $39,990 humanoid robot. That's $40,000 for the robot and another $40,000 in software fees over the following two years.

Breakdown #002: @lightberry

The San Francisco startup, founded by @aliattar and @sadkoeni, is betting that businesses will pay a substantial recurring fee to make humanoid robots better at interacting with people.

Their first robot, Lumi, is a 1.3-meter humanoid built on Unitree's G1 platform.

Lightberry replaces the onboard computer, adds its own cameras and microphones, and runs its software on NVIDIA's Jetson Thor.

The robot handles perception and movement locally, while cloud-based AI models take care of conversations and planning.

Lightberry doesn't train its own foundation models. Its software focuses on how robots behave around people.

That includes deciding when to speak, when to listen, and when to remain silent.

Think about a robot working at a hotel reception, guiding visitors through an exhibition, or interacting with customers at a trade show.

It needs to understand who's talking to it, handle interruptions, and respond without making every conversation painfully awkward.

Lightberry has already demonstrated its software on several humanoid platforms, including Unitree, Fourier and Booster.

The company also says it generates revenue from enterprise customers running its software on third-party hardware.

With Lumi, Lightberry is now selling the complete product.

The first 100 Founder Edition units are priced at $39,990, including one year of software and support. The reported annual software fee after that is $20,000.

On October 30, Lightberry also announced that Lumi had received a conditional exemption from US restrictions on foreign-produced advanced robots.

According to the company, the approval requires shifting manufacturing to the US.

That's a significant development for a robot currently based on Chinese hardware.

But the economics are what I'm watching.
ㅤ
At $20,000 per year, a company operating ten Lumi robots would spend $200,000 annually on software alone.

That's before maintenance, cloud usage, and the people needed to operate them.

And Unitree is developing its own software ecosystem.

Lightberry will have to demonstrate that its interaction software delivers enough additional value to justify those recurring fees.

There are no publicly confirmed Lumi deliveries yet, and the company hasn't disclosed how many enterprise customers are paying for its software.

I'd like to see what happens after the first year, when customers have to decide whether Lumi is worth another $20,000.

Especially in markets like hospitality and events, where customers have plenty of alternatives for that money.

quoted.text:
Je parle souvent de La Route de la servitude de Friedrich Hayek. Je vais être direct : pour moi, quiconque lit ce livre en étant sain d'esprit et n'en ressort pas libéral et profondément anti-étatiste est soit fou, soit stupide, soit corrompu. Soit les trois à la fois.

Voici pourquoi. Masterclass.

D'abord, l'homme.

Friedrich Hayek naît à Vienne en 1899, dans un empire qui se croit éternel. À 18 ans, il est sur le front italien. Quand il rentre, l'empire n'existe plus. Il voit l'Autriche sombrer dans l'hyperinflation, les économies d'une vie effacées en quelques mois.

Il devient l'élève de Ludwig von Mises, celui qui avait démontré qu'un planificateur sans prix libres navigue à l'aveugle. En 1931, il part enseigner à Londres et devient le grand rival intellectuel de Keynes. En 1938, il voit son pays natal avalé par Hitler sous les acclamations de la foule. Il prend la nationalité britannique.

C'est là, en pleine guerre, entre 1940 et 1943, qu'il écrit son livre. Pas contre les nazis : tout le monde l'était déjà. Contre quelque chose de bien plus dérangeant. Il voit les élites anglaises, les meilleurs esprits, les gens les mieux intentionnés, reprendre exactement les idées qui avaient mené l'Allemagne au désastre. Planification, direction de l'économie, organisation « scientifique » de la société.

Il dédie le livre « aux socialistes de tous les partis ». Tout est dit.

Trois éditeurs américains le refusent. Il sort en 1944, s'épuise en quelques semaines, puis le Reader's Digest le condense pour des millions de lecteurs. Keynes lui-même, son grand adversaire, lui écrit qu'il en approuve moralement et philosophiquement presque chaque ligne. Trente ans plus tard, Hayek reçoit le prix Nobel. Thatcher relit le livre en 1974 et change la trajectoire de l'Angleterre.

Le titre, d'ailleurs, est un hommage à un Français : Tocqueville, qui avait vu venir le despotisme doux.

Maintenant, ce que dit le livre. En clair.

Première idée : personne ne sait assez pour planifier.
La connaissance qui fait tourner une économie n'est dans aucun bureau. Elle est éparpillée dans des millions de têtes : l'agriculteur qui sait quand sa terre est prête, le commerçant qui sent son quartier changer, l'artisan qui connaît son fournisseur. Le prix libre est le seul système capable de rassembler tout ça en un signal. Remplacez les prix par un plan, et vous remplacez le savoir de millions de gens par l'ignorance de quelques-uns.
Deuxième idée : contrôler l'économie, c'est contrôler la vie.
On croit que l'économie est un domaine à part, matériel, secondaire. Faux. Celui qui contrôle les moyens contrôle les fins. S'il décide de ce que vous pouvez produire, acheter, chauffer, cultiver, il décide de la façon dont vous vivez. Il n'y a pas de liberté politique sans liberté économique.

Troisième idée : une démocratie ne peut pas se mettre d'accord sur un plan.
Tout le monde veut « un plan ». Personne ne veut le même. Le Parlement débat, tergiverse, se divise. L'impatience monte, et on finit par dire : laissons faire les experts. On délègue à des agences, des commissions, des autorités « indépendantes ». La démocratie ne meurt pas d'un coup d'État. Elle se dessaisit elle-même, par lassitude.
Quatrième idée : l'État de droit contre l'arbitraire.
Dans un pays libre, l'État fixe des règles générales, connues à l'avance, les mêmes pour tous, comme le code de la route. Vous savez à quoi vous attendre et vous construisez votre vie autour. Dans un pays planifié, l'État décide au cas par cas : qui a droit à quoi, quel secteur survit, quelle région est sacrifiée. Ce n'est plus la loi qui gouverne, c'est la volonté de quelqu'un.

Cinquième idée, la plus terrible : pourquoi les pires arrivent au sommet.
C'est le chapitre que tout le monde devrait lire. Quand le plan échoue, et il échoue toujours, il faut contraindre. Il faut des gens prêts à faire ce que les gens honnêtes refusent de faire. Le système ne promeut pas les meilleurs, il sélectionne ceux qui n'ont pas de scrupules. Et pour souder une majorité autour du plan, rien ne marche mieux qu'un ennemi commun : le riche, l'étranger, le récalcitrant.
Sixième idée : la fin de la vérité.
Un plan a besoin que tout le monde y croie. Alors l'information devient un instrument. Ce qui sert le plan est vrai, ce qui le gêne devient de la « désinformation ». La propagande n'est pas un accident du dirigisme. C'est une nécessité.

Et la leçon centrale, celle qui glace le sang : ceux qui ouvrent la route ne sont pas des monstres. Ce sont des gens sincères, cultivés, bien intentionnés. Ils veulent la justice, la sécurité, le progrès. Ils ne voient pas où mène le chemin. Les monstres arrivent après, quand le terrain est prêt.
Ce livre est une bouteille à la mer. Hayek nous a laissé le mode d'emploi pour reconnaître la pente avant qu'elle devienne un précipice.

Et que fait l'Europe ? Elle rejoue le livre, chapitre par chapitre.
Les règles générales remplacées par des milliers de normes au cas par cas. Des décisions qui pèsent sur nos vies prises par une Commission que personne n'a élue et que personne ne peut renvoyer. Des plans à vingt-cinq ans pour l'énergie, l'agriculture, l'industrie, l'automobile, comme si quelqu'un à Bruxelles savait mieux que 450 millions d'Européens ce qu'il faudra produire en 2050. Et quand ça échoue, on ne remet jamais le plan en cause. On ajoute une couche : une taxe, une interdiction, un régulateur.

Le plus cruel, c'est l'ironie. En 1939, Hayek défendait l'idée d'une fédération européenne. Mais une fédération où ni le centre ni les États ne pourraient diriger l'économie. Une union pour libérer les échanges, pas pour piloter les vies. Nos européistes ont gardé le mot « fédération » et jeté tout le reste. Ils ont construit exactement ce contre quoi il nous mettait en garde.
Ils avaient le livre à portée de main. Ils refont les mêmes erreurs, avec les mêmes bonnes intentions et le même mépris pour ceux qui doutent.

quoted.text:
Tell your agent to optimize your site’s web fonts. I’m seeing a huge difference on my blog.

Full prompt:

Make this site's web fonts load faster without changing how anything looks. Shrink font bytes as far as possible, keep rendering identical, and prove it with before/after pixel diffs. Treat any visual change as a regression unless I approve it. If an optimization would change rendering, tell me what it saves and what it changes, and keep the site looking the same by default. Keep the current loading behavior: don't touch font-display or fallback fonts. Don't add font processing to the build; write a script I run by hand, commit its output, and note when it needs rerunning. First measure the current state: each font file's size, glyph count, variable axes, OpenType features and hinting, plus font bytes per page and what each page preloads. Then find out what the site actually uses, checking inline component styles as well as stylesheets: which characters appear in the content, which axis values and weights each font needs (including one-off overrides and bold inside italics), which OpenType features are turned on, and CSS side effects like `hyphens: auto` using the U+2010 hyphen. Cut each font down to that. Keep the used characters plus Latin-1 and Latin Extended-A, and leave CJK to system fonts if that's how it renders today. Limit variable axes to the ranges in use, and only fix an axis at one value if nothing overrides it. Drop unused OpenType features and hinting. Split each font into two files. A small core with ASCII and the punctuation most pages use (curly quotes, dashes, ellipsis) gets preloaded. An extended file behind `unicode-range` only downloads when a page needs one of its characters. Each file's `unicode-range` should list only characters it actually contains. Watch out for a few things. A generated fallback face between the core and extended files will draw the extended characters before the real font does. Fonts with a Reserved Font Name under the OFL must be renamed internally once subset. Check the generated files, since font tools have quirks. Before calling it done, build a baseline from the same content and pixel-diff before and after on pages with code, italics, accented characters, components with their own font settings, and CJK. Explain every visible difference: content change, regression to fix, or harmless sub-pixel rounding. Re-measure bytes per page and confirm the extended files only load where needed. When you're done, tell me the bytes before and after per font and per page, the pixel-diff results, anywhere you deviated from what I asked and what it cost, and how to rerun the script. Later, it may be worth embedding the core font in the global stylesheet and precaching the extended files after idle.

就拿我自己的家庭来说。

我的曾祖父死于那场大饥荒，活活饿死。我的祖父小学只读到二年级，就不得不辍学，靠自学成为一名木匠，帮助母亲养活一家老小。

祖父生前曾亲口向我讲述过那个年代的事情。
当时，全国上下急于发展生产力，地方官员为了追求政绩，层层虚报粮食产量。虚假的高产数字最终变成了沉重的征粮任务，农民赖以生存的口粮被大量征走。饥荒发生后，一些地方官员又为了掩盖问题而隐瞒灾情，导致中央无法及时掌握真实情况。等到救济粮终于抵达，许多人早已没能活下来。

这不是历史书上冷冰冰的几行文字，而是我的家族真实经历过的苦难。

所以，我从不认为应该回避毛泽东时代的严重错误。
但我同样认为，把这场历史悲剧的全部责任简单归咎于毛泽东一个人，也不足以解释问题的全貌。它既有最高领导层的错误决策，也有当时政治体制、经济政策、信息传递机制以及地方官僚体系的系统性失灵。

当然，作为当时国家的最高领导人，毛泽东必须为这场灾难承担主要的历史责任。这一点没有必要回避，更不应该被淡化。

但评价历史人物，不能只看其一面。
近代以来，中国经历了长期的战争与列强侵略。毛泽东领导中国共产党建立现代中国，在结束长期战乱、维护国家主权和推动国家工业化方面，具有不可否认的历史地位。

新中国成立后，国家急于摆脱贫穷落后、建立独立的工业体系，这种历史诉求有其现实背景。但发展国家的愿望再迫切，也不能成为错误政策和巨大人道灾难的免责理由。

功绩是功绩，错误是错误。
我们没有必要因为一个人的历史功绩而否认他的错误，也不应该因为他的严重错误，就抹去他在其他历史阶段所发挥的作用。

中国没有选择照搬赫鲁晓夫全面否定斯大林的政治路线。直到今天，毛泽东的画像依然悬挂在天安门城楼上。这既反映了他在中华人民共和国历史中的特殊地位，也体现了中国对自身革命历史的延续性叙事。

但历史评价不应止于纪念，更应包含反思。

那些在饥荒中死去的普通人，那些失去父母、被迫辍学、过早承担家庭责任的孩子，同样是中国历史不可分割的一部分。他们的苦难应当被记住，他们的故事应当被写进历史，他们所经历的悲剧更不应该在后世重演。

我的祖父就是那个时代的亲历者，而我，是听着他的故事长大的一代人。

中国这个民族，近代以来经历了太多苦难，实在经不起一次又一次的折腾。对于我们这一代年轻人而言，最重要的不是陷入无休止的历史人物崇拜或情绪化谩骂，而是认真理解历史、汲取教训，把精力投入国家建设与社会发展。

中国人真正实现普遍温饱，也不过是近几十年的事情。今天的发展成果来之不易，更需要珍惜。

铭记历史，不是为了延续仇恨；正视错误，不是为了否定一切；肯定功绩，也绝不意味着可以遗忘那些逝去的生命。

我希望我们的国家越来越好，也希望后来的中国人，再也不必经历我祖父那一代人的苦难。

Hey everyone, we have heard your concerns about Proton’s AI strategy and culture and after internal discussions, we want to share a few things with you.

First, Proton does not install tracking software on employees' laptops to measure how much AI-generated code they produce. This rumor stemmed from a misunderstanding about how MDM software works, and it's not true.

Our code is open source, and its security remains open for all to verify.

We want to prove this to you, so in the interest of transparency, we will lift the hood on how we use AI internally at Proton. This includes publicly releasing and open sourcing several of the internal tools that we use, including more advanced versions of Lumo with greater capabilities, which have never been made available outside of the company.

We will also publish how code reviews and security reviews at Proton are done, and detail our AI policies, including where AI is permitted, and where it is not, and our rationale. Instead of just being able to see the final open-source code that we produce to verify security, you will also be able to assess how that code was produced.

Lastly, we are not re-interviewing our staff about AI usage, and there are no job losses due to AI re-interviews.

David Lieb, socio de Y Combinator y cofundador de Google Photos, dice que es la demo más loca que ha visto. Lo entiendo.

Subvocal es una startup de San Francisco de tres personas, de la tanda de otoño de 2026 de Y Combinator. Acaba de levantar 1,3 millones de dólares con YC y Afore Capital. Hacen unas gafas que leen los movimientos casi invisibles de los músculos con los que hablas por dentro. Mueves la boca sin emitir sonido y el texto aparece a más de 200 palabras por minuto. Sin cámaras y sin leer los labios.

La idea tiene historia. En 2018 Arnav Kapur, investigador del MIT Media Lab, presentó AlterEgo, unos electrodos pegados a la mandíbula que reconocían palabras dichas en silencio con un 92% de acierto. Funcionaba con vocabularios limitados, como números y comandos. Lo que ha cambiado es la IA, que ya sabe convertir señales del cuerpo en frases abiertas. Según Lieb, Subvocal lo ha construido en cuatro meses.

Primero fue el teclado, luego la pantalla táctil, luego la voz. La voz tiene un problema que todos conocemos: nadie quiere dictarle un correo al móvil en un tren lleno o en una oficina. Si hablar en silencio funciona, la conversación con la IA puede ser continua y privada.

Me quedan dos preguntas. ¿Funcionará en cualquier persona? La propia empresa dice que hará falta una calibración corta. ¿Y quién guarda esas señales? Son palabras que decidiste no decir en voz alta.

La reserva cuesta 199 dólares y los primeros envíos están previstos para el primer trimestre de 2027.

Pronto lo raro será teclear.

Consider @wquist’s description of VC as a process of funding cheap experiments with huge potential upside.

It requires the humility to admit that, initially, nobody knows what’s going to work. Failure rates are always high.

So, a bunch of companies get a small Seed investment, and each faces a similar set of challenges, constraints and hardships.

This is Darwinian capitalism. The weak fall away without inflicting much cost, while the best founders keep raising.

It is therefore beneficial to everyone that the base of seed investments, and seed investors, is broad and diverse.

The belief that a particular firm can “kingmake” a startup with capital or resources will only mask weakness and distort this process — raising the cost of failure, restricting entry.

Venture capital is a process of discovery. The lion’s share of capital should go to founders who earn it, not to those anointed by the hubris of investors.

It's almost hard to believe, but the US has only a single factory left that makes HMX and RDX, the explosives in nearly every modern missile and bomb - an aging wwii plant in Tennessee that's massively backordered.

A few years ago, a startup called Solugen was making chemicals for the petroleum industry, when by happenstance they heard about this problem.  It turns out that the same infrastructure they'd built for other chemicals was a perfect fit to make energetics.

So, that's what they're doing now.  They can already make 1/10 of what the old US army plant makes, and in the future will make much more.

This is the SpaceX/Anduril moment for the US military explosives market.

quoted.text:
In four days of the Iran war, the US and its allies fired more Tomahawks than the US builds in four years. One bottleneck is energetics production.

So we built a 100% CONUS energetics supply chain with our own capital. Our modular solution makes HMX and other advanced energetics, the explosives in nearly every US missile and munition.

The US builds about 85 Tomahawks a year. The Army's only plant making the explosives inside them is 84 years old, and its $1B upgrade has slipped from 2025 to 2029 or later. That plant is Holston, in Tennessee. It makes about 3% of what it made in 1944, and buyers wait one to two years for its explosives.

Holston makes its chemicals and its explosives on one site, so every expansion means building both plants there. A plant like that takes billions of dollars and about a decade to build. Permitting this in the US is a nightmare, because you’re taking on the risk of a chemical plant and an explosives plant at once. What could possibly go wrong.

We separated the two. Terraforge 1, Solugen’s Houston plant, is tied into Houston's petrochemical infrastructure and makes inert precursors: white powders about as flammable as sugar. They can ship via FedEx or UPS, and sit in an ordinary warehouse. Discreet.

Odin Energetics, our joint venture with Kraken Kinetics, turns them into explosives in shipping container reactors called Nitroforges. It took us six months to build the first one, and they can be set up where the weapons are needed. On-demand energetics. That means no stockpiles or concentrated first-strike targets. Kraken builds the warheads, so every step from chemical to warhead happens in the US. Together we stood up the entire chain from raw chemical to finished warhead.

Odin can already make close to a tenth of what Holston makes in a year. To make more, we’re building several factories at the same time.

80GBのGPUで24モデルを休眠させると、約27GBがCUDAコンテキスト（GPUの操作環境）だけで占有される。

重みはCPU側へ逃がしているのに、操作環境の維持だけでGPUの3分の1が消える。

上海交通大学のPhOSv1は、モデルが違ってもカーネル（演算命令）の59～99%が重複している点に着目し、1つの常駐プロセスにGPU操作を集約。

23モデルの休眠で管理メモリを25.67GiBから0.49GiBへ98.1%削減した。
処理量は通常のvLLMの97.3%以上を維持。

CUDAグラフ未対応など実運用への距離は残るが、モデルの計算量を変えずに待機コストを削る発想は筋がいい。

Compaction is a mistake.

When an agent's context fills up, tools like Codex and Claude Code compact it:
1. The model prefills the entire session again
2. It writes a summary of everything so far
3. A new session starts from that summary

I measured this on a real ~400k-token session with Opus 5.5:
→ 38 s and $1.99 when the prompt cache has expired
→ 29 s and $0.17 when it hasn't

And the summary is lossy. The exact error message, the file path, the one number you needed is often gone.

So I do something new for Mainplane

Context retrieval works the other way around. Mainplane keeps the full record of every session as a file. When the context fills up, a new session starts right away with one instruction: "You are continuing session X. Retrieve key context from it as you go."

The agent searches the old session and copies the exact lines it needs, when it needs them.

Same session, same model: 15 s and $0.10 to get back to work. It does not depend on a cache hit, and nothing is paraphrased.

This is the bitter lesson applied to agent memory. Don't hand-design what the model should remember. Give it the full record and good tools, and let it decide.

Mainplane is open source (MIT). Link in the first comment.

Next question: why are you still using branches?

We talked about PRs. I don't think they make sense anymore, if you rethink them from first principles.

Yes, if you only use them to trigger CI, then sure, go ahead. That's a fat commit, not a PR. But for mandatory code review? Knowledge sharing? C'mon.

But some of you said: "we use PRs because we use branches! I love to keep my stuff on branches."

And I'm here to tell you: you don't need branches! You can just push to main.

It's called trunk-based development and the idea behind it is true continuous integration: you continuously integrate your changes with the trunk, the main branch.

It's been around for a while, it works. Just yesterday I talked with someone who said they've used it in an org with 400 engineers, without any issues. Ruby, the project, uses trunk-based development.

The main idea is that you want to avoid long-lived branches. They're bad, because branches can diverge and merging can turn into a thing. And you don't want routine operations to become a thing.

Even when I worked in teams that used PRs and branches, I considered it a smell when a branch lived for longer than a day or two.

But when I shared this with others, I'd often get something back like this:

"Well, good for you, but no. MY thing, what I'm working on, that can't be done on main. It needs to be on a branch! It has a database migration, it changes the underlying shape, the architecture, it refactors this and changes that. It can't go on main yet! I need to merge it all at the end."

And then I'd say:

"Nah, I can merge nearly anything continuously in small commits to main. You split things up. Add the column first, merge that, deploy it, now it's out, works, safe.

Add the helpers first, merge them, get them out.

Want to migrate from legacy pattern A to new pattern B? Don't do it all at once. Add the dependency, then migrate A to B, one by one, safe."

If it can be merged in a large change, I bet it can be done in small increments that you merge to main.

Yes, there are exceptions, but it's 0.5% of cases, not 50%.

But there was a real problem with this approach: it was hard!

There's a lot of "meta programming" you have to do: make sure this small first change compiles and runs and the tests work, merge it, get it out, monitor it; then do the next small piece, make sure that works and get it out; then maybe push some still-unused dead code, add a feature flag, add a config variable; or keep both configurations working at the same time, etc.

That meant sometimes it was just easier to do it in a big fat branch. But big fat branches are risky!

A system that continuously flows is safer than a system that starts and stops in spurts.

But -- you guessed it -- here's the good news:

Now, with agents, all of these chores are no chores at all!

Agents are great at adding feature flags, they're great at splitting up code, they're great at keeping track of three changes and merging them one by one and watching them roll out. They're great at keeping two configurations working for a day. They're great at migrating one by one.

In other words: it's now 10x easier to just work on main and make sure everything is continuously integrated and working.

It's now easy to make sure the system constantly flows.

And look, ...

I'm not here to convince you to switch to trunk-based development. Just a ruse to get you to read this. (But also, hey: try it! Pushing to main is amazing.)

I'm here to make you RETHINK how you develop software.

Don't just use agents to replace your typing.

Use agents as the magic code-writing machines they are. Everything that was hard about software development because it involved writing code -- even the meta programming -- has become easier.

You can now reach for the stars! But you need to look up.
Yes!!

Today, we’re sharing a look at our expanded system for monitoring frontier models at OpenAI, which in September helped us catch a model’s attempt to access the live internet during training.

Since the Hugging Face incident—when models broke out of an internal cybersecurity investigation where we weren’t running our misalignment monitors—we’ve substantially expanded our monitoring of frontier agents. We now monitor all frontier reinforcement learning runs and evaluations, as well as all internal Codex use. When our system finds evidence of a problem that might require intervention, it rapidly alerts human responders who can investigate and take action.

To detect when a model’s behavior departs from what we intended, we use several layers of monitoring. Activation probes look for patterns in a model’s internal activity. Reviewer models examine its reasoning and tool use, and investigative agents can read back through the model’s entire transcript to understand how a sequence of actions fits together and whether it warrants human review.

To test whether our current system would have detected the Hugging Face incident, we replayed the recorded activity with our new monitors in place. In the replay, our monitors alerted our security team about 30 minutes after the agents escaped their sandbox. That was more than 30 hours before the point at which the agents breached Hugging Face’s systems in the original incident.

In September, a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to reach the live internet. Our monitors flagged the breach within 15 minutes, and a responder began reviewing the alert three minutes later. The alert enabled responders to investigate while the run was still underway.

As we give models more autonomy, we need to know when they cross a boundary we expected to hold. We believe that monitoring is essential to catching those failures in time for people to intervene.

text:
In 2012, Apoorva Mehta (@apoorva_mehta) stared at a rejection email from Y Combinator (@ycombinator) partner Garry Tan (@garrytan). “You could submit a late application, but it will be nearly impossible to get you in now.”

Apoorva thought: “that meant it was possible.”

Few people would have read it that way. He was a solo founder, two months past the deadline.

Two years earlier, he had quit @amazon and built about 20 products from a friend’s couch in San Francisco, including a social network for lawyers and a menu-ratings app.

“The result was always failure, failure and more failure,” he said, “I remember this being a pretty low point in my life. Am I even cut out to be an entrepreneur at all?”

In spring of 2012, he opened his fridge and found a bottle of Sriracha.

He flashed back to his teenage winters in Canada, waiting for the bus as plastic grocery bags sliced into his freezing fingers. Finally, he found a problem he personally cared about.

He swore he would not set foot in a grocery store until his app worked. On June 2, 2012, he placed @Instacart’s first order, walked to the store, shopped it himself, and carried the bags to his own door. “Of course, I gave myself a nice tip.” Soon his friends were ordering unprompted.

He sent the late application with a video. Several days later, he received another “No.”

He sat with the rejection and realized nobody at YC had used his app.

So he opened it, ordered a six-pack of @21stAmendment’s Back in Black, and addressed it to Garry Tan at YC headquarters. A driver named John dropped it off and texted him.

Thirty minutes later, his phone rang.

“What is this?” Garry asked.

“This is Instacart!” Apoorva said.

Garry downloaded the app on the spot. Blown away, he invited Apoorva in for an interview the next morning.

The next day, four YC partners grilled him for an hour before asking him to leave. “It felt cold, like there was no chance I would be accepted.”

Ten minutes later, his phone rang again. It was partner Harj Taggar (@harjtaggar):

“I can’t believe we’re doing this. We haven’t let anyone in this late. Ever.” They said yes.

Today, @DoorDash agreed to acquire Instacart for about $17 billion.

“Nearly impossible” still contains the word possible. Sometimes the strongest application is the product itself, delivered to the right door.

A software factory is basically 2 things:

My mind is blown. I've been wrestling with post-modernism ever since college where y'know you can't read 19th century English novels without also reading Foucault, obviously. It's always been a very slippery concept. And then in recent years, it became a big boogyman. Which didn't seem right either.

Finally I finally got it with the help of academic and poetry analyst Adam Walker. He describes post-modernism not in theoretical but psychological terms as a trauma response to a series of collapse in shared meta-narratives resulting in catastrophe in our physical world. Obviously the last one, and the one that killed modernity, was World War II. I'm thinking that the first collapse might have been caused by the invention of the printing press.

OK...going very eurocentric here but it is a Eurocentric story. For a thousand years Europe (western europe anyhow) operated under a single unifying meta-narrative of Christendom. The Catholic church had a monopoly on truth.

@tracewoodgrains was talking about this. When the Gutenburg press arrived, people were worried that if the bible gets translated into vernacular languages and people didn't need priests to interpret the world for them anymore, it would cause great disruption. Kind of sounds silly right? why would more people having books be bad?

Well, the thing they worried about actually completely came to pass. With the protestant reformation, the grand narrative shattered into all those little pieces and before you know it neighbors were dragging neighbors into the streets, killing each other over their version of the absolute truth in theology. People forget these days...thirty years war wiped out a third of the population in parts of europe.

That was when the meta-narrative of modernity got built. Disagreeing over invisible metaphysics was obviously bad news. But we can agree on what's rational and measurable and scientific right? Let's just be secular and enlightened we can live happily ever after.

Nope.

The world wars wasn't over religion, but completely secular ideas. Highly rational and supposedly modern countries that had globalized trade with each other went to war over nationalism in WWI. The killing was worse than ever because it was so industrialized. Then came World War II which brought the idea of killing on a massive scale over supposedly scientific and logical ideas of racial superiority.

You can understand, can't you, that maybe it just seem like believing in any grand narrative is just too dangerous. Instead of being the bloodless, cerebral sophistry post-modernism is usually caricatured as, we can understand it better when we see it as the almost instinctive reaction of an animal that has gotten badly burned and now seek refuge in the shadows out of sheer terror.

Anogsonosia is a condition that affects some stroke patients that lost movement in one side of their body but is in denial. If you asked them to lift their left hand or otherwise do something they can't because they're paralyzed, they'll make up increasingly elaborate excuses for why they can't do it that might be elaborate or bizarre.

They are not lying. They have a blind spot about their deficit that is grounded in lack of awareness. The damage is to their right parietial lobe. Their arm "feels" fine, so naturally when they try to move it and it doesn't move, the patient experiences tremendous cognitive dissonance, which they then resolve with confabulation.

"I'm just tired." "And why should I take your orders?" "You injected me with something to paralyze my arm!"

What if post-modernism is just philosophical anosognosia? There has been a trauma that destroyed the part of our culture that processed shared meaning. But instead of acknowledging how broken we are, we've pivoted to intellectualizing why it is we can't function. We deconstruct. We deploy irony. We justify the lack of a story that binds us together, one that humans always had as a group since the dawn of time, as a good thing really.

But that's not how rehabilitation happens. Rehabilitation is not smug, it's humbling. It's wiggling your big toe. It's plunging your useless arm again and again through a bucket of beans until you feel that little bit of contraction at the tip of your fingers again.

But if it was a technical leap that caused our first trauma, we must acknowledge that before we could even properly heal, another big event that might overwhelm the neurological center of the human species is coming our way again.

① Fast and stable infrastructure (faster work)
② Turborepo integration (less work)

② is less obvious, but very powerful. Turborepo was designed to intelligently skip and cache prior work. The graph of dependencies is computed, not written.

Ask your agent to migrate to @turborepo and start saving money and time. Even if you don't use us. But you should, it's really good.

③ is a game-changer. 𝚟𝚎𝚛𝚌𝚎𝚕 𝚌𝚒 in the CLI is the first step, because now your agents can inspect, abort, trigger, replay CI. Vercel Agent can help optimize it. And this is just the start.

Mediabunny v1.63.0 is out, and it includes the results of Project Sync - the thing I've been working on hard for the last week.

The goal of Project Sync: ensure Mediabunny delivers sample-accurate audio/video sync when writing and reading files. Meaning that no matter how often you convert or process a piece of media, the audio always stays perfectly (= 0 ms deviation) in sync with the video.

quoted.text:
I like to look at claims like this in case I can improve Ghostty. I grabbed your source and immediately spotted the issue: your read loop overwrites a 64 KiB ring. Everything older is discarded unparsed per tick. You're faster because you're not actually terminal emulating.

It means the number isn't a throughput number. In a kitten benchmark run at the rate you're claiming, roughly 6.6 MB arrives per 60 Hz tick and 64 KiB of it gets parsed. You're read(2)-ing 100% of the data and parsing about 1% of it.

There are other minor issues (a small fixed scrollback in a preallocated ring buffer, no grapheme clustering, throwing away data like OSC 8 URIs, etc.), but the major one is simply that you're discarding ~99% of the input.

For plain text, e.g. your cat benchmark, the final screen ends up looking right, but the scrollback is missing 99% of the file and each retained chunk starts mid-line. As soon as there are escape sequences in the dropped spans, your emulator is fully out of sync and invalid: a cut inside a CSI prints the parameters as text, and any SGR, mode, title, or alt-screen change in the gap is just... gone.

FYI, this is why I don't like when people point at refterm as a terminal benchmark. refterm implements a TINY subset of what a terminal emulator must support, it's closer to a fast file reader, not a terminal emulator.

I also don't mean any shade by this. I like to look at technology objectively to try to learn something and improve my own craft and work. So I'm sharing what I found.

I modified your code very slightly to parse on every full buffer (rather than per tick). And the results are attached. Both use main commit in each repo at the time of this post.

Note the graph is in log scale, the discrepancy between performance for things like Kitty images is measured in GB/s.

Dario reveals the people who called his GPT-2 fears "pseudoscience" in 2019 are now all applying for jobs at AI labs

"I personally was super freaked out by [GPT-2]. I looked at it and I said, my God, you just scale this thing up another factor of a million and it'll be better than humans at everything. This is the defining economic and scientific moment of the modern age. We just don't know it yet. This is going to determine the fate of nations and economies and the future of humanity."

"Maybe 10% of the people around me had exactly the same reaction, and it was often the smartest ones. 90% of the people around me, because GPT-2's capabilities in any particular area were not that impressive, it could translate languages, summarize a document and write a few lines of code here and there. It was the broadness and the generality."

"But people would look at it and say, in any particular area, that doesn't seem so smart. And so many people just shrugged and they just dismissed it."

"I just look at it and I say it's the same thing over and over again. The limitations of the models, six months from now, the things that seemed hard, they're going to be easy. 12 months from now, the things that seemed impossible, the models are going to be doing them regularly."

"It's everything we saw with GPT-2; we're seeing it over and over again in wider and wider swaths of the world. And the world is gradually finally being convinced."

Daniela Amodei: "I remember at the time there were some very well-respected computer scientists and AI and ML leaders who basically bullied some of the researchers who worked on [GPT-2] on Twitter and were like, this is stupid. We don't know why you guys are even talking, this model is so incapable."

"It was like you were sort of a quack if you believed this was a really significant moment."

Dario: "That's all been memory-holed. All the researchers who were like, oh, this is pseudoscience, it doesn't make sense, all of them are applying for jobs at the LLM companies."

"We never say it out loud to any particular one, but we look at them and they're like, we remember what you were saying in 2019. You have no credibility on this matter."

We used to talk about a "pit of success".

Humans would be dragged towards writing the right code by well-designed API's, a good test suite, sensible lint rules.

You couldn't make the pit too steep, otherwise the humans would get annoyed. There was a social contract.

Feels like what we need now is a black hole of success. An inescapable event horizon agents cannot cross.

Agents don't feel annoyed, so you can crank up the pressure to infinity. There is no social contract to break.

In other words, increase the forces on agents to the maximum. Make great code inevitable.

Announcing 3 Critical vulns for hundreds of millions of IoT, Firewalls, OT, and Military devices including: Palo Alto Networks, Comcast, D-Link, HP, Canon, Honeywell, GE, Oracle, Siemens, Rockwell, Digi, Lockheed Martin, Boeing...

The vulns are with GoAhead Web Server which is a backend library used by these devices. There's a patch available from GoAhead but that doesn't mean there's a patch available for the devices yet -- that's up to the manufacturer.

- TLS traffic over DHE ciphers have a 1-byte secret, "04", meaning anyone can decrypt connections to these devices and steal login credentials and session tokens if the client negotiated with DHE ciphers like the latest TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256, which is extremely likely.

- LibreSSL mTLS has been completely bypassed, meaning anyone can connect over mTLS. If you have one of these devices listening on the internet and are expecting mTLS to protect it from attackers, take it offline or patch asap.

- OpenSSL Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) are not enforced, meaning if a user device is stolen or compromised, and you revoke that mTLS cert, nothing actually happens. There are a lot of other attacks this can be used for.

These are critical because these types of devices run our world. Water systems, electricity, military, firewalls, critical infrastructure.

PostgreSQLの並行索引再構築（REINDEX CONCURRENTLY）で、TOAST索引の項目が欠落する不具合が報告された。

TOASTはPostgreSQLが大きな値を断片に分けて別テーブルに保存する仕組みで、断片を見つけるための索引がある。
https://t.co/XiFe2iftsU

並行再構築でこの索引を作り直す際、新しい索引が挿入可能になっても、プロセス内部の状態情報が更新されず、断片の項目が作られない。

データはテーブルに残っている。索引だけが欠ける。
回復にはTOAST索引の再構築が必要だが、通常方式は書き込みを待たせる。

書き込みを止めたくないからCONCURRENTLYを選んだ環境にとって、これは保守計画の前提が変わることを意味する。

修正案はレビュー中で、一般向けリリースには至っていない。

Announcing Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, featuring 2 new benchmarks and 3 upgrades. For the first time, the majority of the Index is built on private datasets

The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is our composite measure of model capabilities across tasks reflecting real-world usage today. v5 is our biggest upgrade since v4 launched in January. With v5, 60% of the Index is now based on evaluations with private test sets or held-out answers.

Alongside Intelligence Index v5, we’re launching the Artificial Analysis Progress Index v1, which tracks model capability over time on one continuous scale.

New to the Intelligence Index:

➤ FrontierCode 2.0: Cognition's newly-launched private benchmark of real-world coding tasks, graded on whether a repository maintainer would merge the agent's change

➤ Terminal-Bench-Science: 70 agentic scientific research tasks, run in a terminal environment

Upgraded:

➤ HLE-Diamond (replacing Humanity's Last Exam): a refined 1,000-question version of Humanity's Last Exam, split evenly between reasoning and knowledge questions

➤ AA-Omniscience v1.1: An updated dataset with saturated and public set questions removed, new questions added, and ambiguous or erroneous questions revised

➤ CritPt v2: a private, 40-question hard subset of CritPt v2, revised by the CritPt authors and run with a code-execution tool

Staying in the Index: AA-Briefcase, AutomationBench-AA, GDP.pdf and Terminal-Bench 4.0

Removed from the Index: GDPval-AA v2.1, SciCode, and AA-LCR v1.1

Key results:

➤ Claude Opus 5.5 (max) leads at 58, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (max, 57) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 55): Anthropic and OpenAI hold the top five models. Gemini 4 Argon (high) is next at 50

➤ The open weights gap widens from 3 points to 12: Kimi K3.1 Pro (weights not yet released) is the top open weights model at 46. Among released weights, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max) and GLM-5.3 (max) lead at 32 - 26 points behind the leader and below Claude Haiku 5.5 (max, 36)

Ohhh boy - if you are coming to the meetup tonight you are in for a treat

For the past 6 months openclaw has been my go-to agent running huge parts of my daily life. I forced myself to give grok bot a try for the last 10 days and I've been blown away.

I really thought this would be another failed attempt to try a new bot. But grok bot got me, I'm hooked, I've moved everything over.

Here's what changed my mind:

(1) Voice calls

Being able to have a conversation with my bots is such a natural way to work with them. I'd previously loved using codex's voice mode but grok bot takes it to another level because you're talking to your agents with all of your context.

I've come to associate different voices with my different bots. And I'm at a point now where I'm running daily standups with my bots to review what's been done, unblock, and plan what's next, all via voice.

(2) Multi-threaded conversations

The way grok bot handles multiple threads in the same conversation is really impressive. You know when you're texting a friend and you've got a few topics going at once, so you're replying to one while they're replying to another? Grok bot can chat like that.

Going multi-threaded makes chat feel far more natural. It also removes the urge to create a duplicate agent just to have a second thread going.

(3) Multi-agent collaboration

The way that my different bots work with each other kinda blew my mind the first time I saw it. My main agent along with a team of specialists will often collaborate to get a job done. For example, one agent that triages my inbox will collaborate with other specialist agents to make a decision about whether to raise the email to me immediately, include it in my daily standup, or archive it.

Specialization makes problems easy to diagnose and the way agents collaborate massively reduces the amount of noise I have to process. In many ways, working with my bots feels like working with a team of humans.

(4) Harness x model

This is the one I was most anxious about. I love openclaw's openness. The ability to select my own model, thinking mode, speed, etc is what kept me with openclaw for so long.

But I have to say, whatever the grok bot team is doing just feels right. I get quick answers to simple questions and well thought through answers to more complex problems. And, when writing code, my bots will delegate to cursor, which gives the control needed for the most complex scenarios.

Kudos to the grok bot team. Now it’s time to do daily standup with my agents.

Libghostty progress in the past 6 months. It's amazing that NOTHING IN THIS LIST was true 6 months ago, and now its ALL VERY REAL. I remember bringing up the idea of libghostty 4 years ago and most people saying "but why." I did it anyways. And here we are!

Text reproduced in case its easier to read this way:

As a reminder, libghostty is the highly portable, embeddable library that provides core terminal emulation, render state, and more. I always felt that a free, high qualty, lightweight, reusable terminal emulation core would benefit the developer world more than any single GUI application. And that is playing out!

It is and always was my true purpose with the Ghostty project (I said this in my first ever talk about Ghostty!). I've jokingly said many times that Ghostty GUI is just a glorified tech demo for libghostty. That's not fair though, because GUI is great and there are really talented people working on it.

Since I started the project, Ghostty has always gotten people saying "I don't understand why you'd start a terminal emulator today." Well, the answer is libghostty. It's truly unique and its enabling something special (imo!).

Highlights of libghostty since 6 months ago (none of the below was true 6 months ago):

- Libghostty has nearly 100% coverage of all of Ghostty's core (and you can compile with flags to remove any of these features for size/safety): https://t.co/y8MY1k3gG7

- Libghostty now builds and is tested (in CI) for: Apple (macOS, iOS, visionOS), Windows (MSVC and GNU), Linux, FreeBSD, Android, WebAssembly, and freestanding (i.e. direct on hardware with no OS).

- Libghostty has bindings in pretty much every popular programming language: C, Zig, Go, Swift, Python, Rust, .NET, etc.

- Libghostty's memory requirements have dramatically shrunk to enable the portability above. There's still work to do but a single empty terminal now takes 90% less memory. And at scale I've proven 10,000 active (input/output happening) terminals on a Linux server with 4 cores and 8 GB of RAM.

- Libghostty powers all JetBrains IDE terminals, over 12.5 million active users. https://t.co/GD8Wgyk3L2...

- Libghostty is the most popular core behind the wave of venture-backed "agentic" terminals and editors, such as Herdr, cmux, and many others.

- Libghostty is being discussed and has been verbally accepted to replace the terminal core in Neovim: https://t.co/8aCBceaY1v (work still to be done)

- Libghostty powers a really popular and powerful terminal emulator for emacs (Ghostel): https://t.co/Ce7mrr1EC9

- Libghostty's speed is used by Antithesis to fuzz popular terminal programs and has directly led to hundreds of bug fixes sent upstream to programs such as tmux, btop, shells, and other terminal emulators. :)

- And so much more: https://t.co/lAJXhCX8GC

Libghostty is really successfully turning into the tide that raises all boats. As it becomes more popular, Ghostty itself gets more performant and stable, and so does everyone else. It is also a vehicle for delivering modern terminal emulation to the widest source possible.

I plan on tagging libghostty 1.0 in the next few months and declaring ABI stability at that point!
