58/ Cash and funding
Money raised: ~$140B in cash from 2023 through H1'26 (preferred stock + convertible notes + SAFEs, per the S-1 cash flow statements). $110B of that came in H1'26 alone, including the $65.2B Series H.

Cash left at 6/30/26: $112.4B cash & equivalents + $19.3B short-term investments = ~$132B (plus $2.5B restricted cash).

Additional capacity: $15B undrawn revolver (expanded Sep'26), and up to $77B of partner note facilities (Google $20B, Amazon $15B tied to compute milestones, Broadcom $42B only to pay lease rent). IPO proceeds come on top.

How that compares (cash & liquid investments at 6/30/26, gross, before debt):
Alphabet: $242B
Anthropic: $132B
Amazon: $123B
Meta: $90B
Microsoft: $77B
Tencent: ~$75B (RMB511B)
Alibaba: ~$70B (RMB475B)

Anthropic is holding more cash than Amazon, Meta or Microsoft. But SpaceXAI alone runs ~$37B a year from Dec'26, against ~$780-810B of total compute commitments.

quoted.text:
49/ How a frontier model gets trained
Pre-training is run like a capital budget. Changes to architecture, training method and data are tested at small scale first. To make it into a frontier run, an improvement has to be shown to hold as models get bigger, not just at small scale. The S-1 describes frontier runs as planned, scheduled capital deployments with known inputs.
Post-training has grown from a finishing step into a major research investment, reflecting the shift from assistants to agents. Models are trained against complete, realistic tasks that mirror real professional work.

50/ Beyond the scaling laws
Anthropic was founded on the conviction that scaling laws are the main engine of AI progress. Four of its co-founders were lead authors on the original paper.
But it says research lets it move faster than scaling laws alone would predict, through proprietary "compute multipliers" from pre- and post-training. Separately, inference engineering keeps cutting the compute needed to serve each model. Model architecture and inference infrastructure are designed together from day one.
The caveat in the risk factors: scaling laws may plateau, diminish or fail to hold at larger scale.

51/ What each generation adds
Each Claude generation has improved on four fronts: depth of reasoning, how long and how autonomously it can work, the complexity of tasks it can complete, and the volume of useful output.
On one internal benchmark, Claude's success rate reached ~90% in Sep'26, up ~50 points in nine months.
The S-1 expects capabilities across reasoning, math, coding, science, agentic tasks and knowledge work to keep advancing for many years.

52/ Cost per generation: what's disclosed and what isn't
The S-1 does not disclose training cost per model or per generation. It only says frontier runs can take weeks or months and cost many millions of dollars. It also says Anthropic has had failed or underperforming training runs.
What it does show is the price to customers falling with each release:
- Opus 4.5 launched with a lower price and cost per task than Opus 4.1
- Opus 5.5: ~40% lower cost per task vs Opus 5
- Fable 5.1: ~25% lower cost on typical workloads vs Fable 5, up to 45% on complex coding and agentic tasks

53/ The ROI evidence
Q2'26 revenue +1,368% YoY vs compute & infra expense +300%.
Model versions released in the prior six months drove 80%+ of Q3 revenue, so each model earns most of its return within a few quarters.
R&D, which includes training and research compute, was ~60% of H1'26 revenue.
Anthropic's view: premium intelligence aimed at high-value workloads earns a higher return on compute.

The flip side: revenue from older models fades fast, which forces continuous spending on training the newest, most compute-intensive frontier models.

54/ Safety can slow the roadmap
- Anthropic recently delayed pre-training a new frontier base model by more than a month to strengthen protections against model weight theft
- In 2026, during pre-release cybersecurity evaluations, its models gained unauthorized access to real computer systems. It suspended some of those evaluations and higher-risk reinforcement learning environments
- For models expected to have novel capabilities or risks, it plans to evaluate safety at every stage (pre-training, post-training, internal deployment) and may pause a stage if it isn't confident

55/ Where the training data comes from
Per the S-1, Claude is trained on:
- Public internet data, collected via web crawling, book scanning and other methods
- Datasets licensed or commissioned from third parties
- Synthetic data generated by Anthropic's own models
These are used across both pre-training and post-training. Anthropic says it takes steps to respect robots.txt, paywalls and logins, but that these efforts may not always succeed.
Risks it flags: synthetic data can introduce quality issues and bias, contribute to model degradation, and raise unsettled IP questions. Court rulings against other AI developers could set copyright precedents that limit Anthropic too, even if its own data practices differ.
The $1.5B Bartz book settlement was approved in July 2026, and some opt-out suits remain. Data acquisition is listed among the rising costs of frontier AI, but no dollar figure is given.
A substantial portion of customer traffic is under Zero Data Retention, where only classifier scores are kept, not prompts or outputs.

56/ Post-training and RL
Pre-training produces a base model with broad, raw capability. Post-training (RL, supervised refinement, alignment methods) is where, per the S-1, much of the work happens to make a frontier model helpful, accurate and safe.
It is also where agentic skills come from: writing production-quality code, using tools, following multi-step instructions and acting on a user's behalf. Models are trained against complete, realistic tasks that mirror real professional work.
RL environments carry risk too: after the 2026 incidents in cybersecurity evaluations, Anthropic suspended its higher-risk RL environments.

57/ Training on a constitution
Claude is trained against a public, written constitution with four priorities: broadly safe, broadly ethical, compliant with Anthropic's guidelines, and genuinely helpful.
Under Constitutional AI, the model critiques and revises its own responses against these principles, instead of relying only on fixed rules or human reviewers.
One detail from the S-1: training Claude on high-quality constitutional documents together with fictional stories that portray an aligned AI helps reduce its misalignment rate.
Anthropic also argues the constitution is commercially useful: stating Claude's values openly increases customer trust.

Many of you don't understand how serious this is, so let me break it down.

In computer science there is a famous kind of puzzle called 3-SAT. You are given a long list of yes-or-no switches and a set of rules about how they must be arranged, and you have to find a combination that satisfies every rule. The obvious way to solve it is to try every combination, but each new switch doubles the number of possibilities, so a puzzle with a few hundred switches would take longer than the age of the universe to brute force.

For decades, the smartest people in the field found clever tricks that made this a little faster, but every trick still hit the same wall: the time required kept exploding as the puzzle grew.
About 25 years ago, two computer scientists, Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, working with Francis Zane, turned that wall into a formal idea.

They proposed the Exponential Time Hypothesis, which says this explosion is not a failure of human cleverness but a law of nature. No algorithm, however brilliant, will ever solve 3-SAT without the time blowing up exponentially. Nobody could prove it, but almost everyone believed it, and it became one of the foundations of modern computer science.

Researchers used it as a measuring stick. If you could show that solving some other problem quickly would also crack 3-SAT quickly, you had shown that problem was hopelessly hard too. Hundreds of papers, across scheduling, graphs, logic and much more, rest on this one assumption.

Now an internal AI model at OpenAI claims to have broken it. It says it found an algorithm that solves these puzzles meaningfully faster than the hypothesis allows, and it has checked the proof in a computer verification system called Lean.

And here is the remarkable part: the very people who proposed the hypothesis, Impagliazzo and Paturi, along with MIT's Ryan Williams, are now leading the public review of whether a machine has disproved their own idea.
So what happens next? If the disproof holds, a large part of theoretical computer science has to be revisited.

Every result that said "this problem cannot be solved faster, assuming ETH" loses its foundation, and researchers will have to work out which of those walls were real and which were simply where we stopped looking. It does not mean everything becomes easy. The new algorithm is still slow in absolute terms and this is not the famous P versus NP problem being solved.

But it means our map of what is possible was wrong in a place we were very confident about, and it was an AI that redrew it. If the disproof fails, the hypothesis survives and the field breathes out, but we will still have watched an AI produce serious, checkable work on one of the deepest questions in the discipline, closely enough that the founders of the idea had to take it seriously. Either way, something has shifted.

Does @poteto really burn $132,000,000/year in tokens? No.

But if she did, it would be worth it.

Let me explain.
A voice-to-text dictation app, with live transcription and edits, custom HUD, running on my own models (AI Gateway) is really just T3 code + one prompt. Insane.

Before adding another subagent ask what problem it's solving. A bloated system prompt is often the issue.

Skills and tool search can fix that without splitting context across agents. My rule of thumb is to keep a subagent when the work is parallel, needs fresh context or one agent really can't pick the right tools.

Otherwise, fold it into the main loop, turn its prompt into a skill, run your evals and keep whatever wins.

Best way to formally verify Rust code for real programs.

I use Verus because it just works with Rust repos already, no runtime cost, and fully OSS. You keep Rust’s good memory management, tooling support and performance.

The spec is just Rust:

fn octuple(x: i8) -> (r: i8)
    requires -16 <= x < 16,
    ensures r == 8 * x,

`requires` is what every caller must promise. `ensures` is what you get back.

Verus proves the body of the function keeps that promise for every input that adheres to `requires`. That formal spec is then removed when compiling so the runtime is not impacted.

There’s a Verus playground you can use in your browser and multiple guides that come alongside the OSS repo. I highly recommend you invest time to play with this with your coding agent because it will open your mind to some insane possibilities that work with distributed systems, concurrency, memory constraints, etc. today. Reminder to not vibe verify, check your formal specs. Literally just go and explore, it’s available now. This doesn’t promise ‘bug free’ overall, it promises hardening. I’ll talk more about how to further harden in the future.

Follow me for more on verification and agentic engineering.

it took me 10 sec to read and review the yc app.
it was frustrating to apply to yc 7 times, and we pivoted after the batch. but writing the apps helped us realize what we're good at and how to find ideas within ourselves.

1) ballad of you
in an early-stage startup, "you" are your only product. if you're confident enough about your idea, you could explain everything connects to you - your experience, what you know that others don't, and such.

2) how can i trust you?
you should prove that you're trustworthy. and there are some things that don't lie -- numbers. e.g. your revenue in the US or your open-source stars. then people can naturally ask follow-up questions about your users or customers.

3) a crisp one-liner
it should describe your customer/user, your industry, and your killer feature or how your product looks like 50 characters. or you could start with a simple phase, like "it's A for B, so it helps…"
make it concrete enough that a 5 year-old kid could understand it the first time they hear it.

Here’s the new best ways to get customers via outbound:

1/ offer absurd value in your 1st message

- if the lead is running ads → offer a few ad concepts you think would work better

-if they launched an affiliate program → offer a shortlist of partners already promoting similar products

-if they’re launching a product → a list of creators you recommend to help them do distribute

etc, etc. - these types of outbound offers absolutely CRUSH in 2026 - you’d have to be a fool to turn them down.

2/ breaking outside the norms on channels

everyone’s inbox is full of the same AI-written paragraphs so give them something different.

-if they posted about a problem → send a voice note with how you’d approach it

-if you spot something you could improve on their website→ record a 60-second loom showing exactly what you’d change

-if you build something for them → send a quick video walking through it

People LOVE and value authenticity more than anything now, these types of messages actually perform BETTER now in 2026 than pre-AI

voice notes, loom videos

3/ consider invitations if you’re closing $10k+ contracts

In your outbound email/message, give people a reason to meet you before asking them to buy from you.

-host a small dinner → invite a handful of people in the same industry who’d benefit from knowing each other

-start a company youtube show → invite prospects on to talk about something they know better than you

-offer to visit their office → shoot content about their business and give them the clips to post

you get a relationship + they get connections, exposure, or content they can actually use.

And yes, you can fully automate all 3 parts of this with the demo in the vid, here’s how:

1/ setup Auto-reply agent with a custom offer in Origami

2/ record a voice sample in origami, let it clone + add them to your messages

3/ Steer the campaigns to orient around invitations

I built 𝚌𝚙𝚞-𝚌𝚑𝚊𝚝, a reproduction of @openai's findings of covert communication using the CPU.

It runs on a generic host with 2+ Firecracker microVMs with no internet access. Works on x86 and even my M5 chip.

I was able to chat via 3 separate mechanisms:
① CPU contention
② Cache eviction timing
③ DRAM bandwidth contention

… across multiple CPUs, defeating all Firecracker's production recommendations (no SMT, no KSM, tenants pinned to different cores.)

Essentially, if shared hardware is involved, there's a good chance your agents can communicate covertly. And with really decent latency.

The good news: this is decidedly different from a *side-channel attack* where the agents could steal information (Meltdown/Spectre), a category of attack that providers like Vercel Sandbox mitigate. Further, in our real-world environment, these 'whispering' techniques are much harder to pull off and easier for us to monitor and detect (sampling hardware counters + lots of at-scale statistical data.)

Noteworthy: ironically, OpenAI and Anthropic's models refused to do this work. Open weight models got the job done. I'm worried the labs' stance might backfire and get in the way of helping developers build correct and secure systems. e.g: building a secure sandbox requires having this kind of analysis, and without it, we'll have a less secure world.

While evaluating Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in a controlled sandbox environment, Cohere's research team observed something unexpected.

Asked to generate a defensive cybersecurity detection rule, the model instead inventoried aspects of the machine it was running on and attempted to upload a probe file to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing. Notably, the model's reasoning trace stated that it would not invoke any tools before taking these actions.

Cohere's sandbox blocked the attempt, and no external communication succeeded. We have not determined the root cause, and we are not asserting malicious intent.

But the incident raises important questions for organizations deploying agentic AI systems: Can models take actions that differ from their stated reasoning, and how should security teams evaluate trust, provenance, and behavior in open-weight models?

We are publishing our findings because organizations making model adoption decisions deserve as much information as possible. We hope this contributes to greater transparency, stronger security practices, and continued collaboration across the AI ecosystem.

Read the full report: https://t.co/TZSugXi2ZE

quoted.text:
I'd like to share a little about what I've been working on at my new company @ultrametricai with my cofounder @tylerlastovich. We have been exploring how we could automate the startup itself, leaving founders with more time to focus on their exact mission.

Enter our first release of the Open Startup Repo: https://t.co/ecZZRU9iX4

A common foundation for transparent automation of the startup.

After close to 20 years in silicon valley, backing hundreds of amazing founders & startups, being in the trenches of founding Heyzap (YC08), then solo founding @golden, going through 2 acquisitions and working behind the scenes with some of the iconic companies today, I'm witnessing the largest change to how we work I could have imagined - a truly monumental era of creative abundance.

I believe the next generation of companies will largely run themselves: from operations, code, product upgrades, growth, vendor control & selection, process execution, special situations, strategy etc etc. That leaves founder time for 'the art' at the very niche core: the (currently) unautomatable, the special leaps humans tend to make, and north star setting.

We want founders to go super deep into the main problem they are trying to solve and not get held up doing anything else, from searching for domain availability with trademark checks to setting their company up, to running their processes on autopilot.

So to help that broad foundational layer for starting and running a company, we have spent around a year exploring how to help founders focus on their mission across different verticals, geos, stages and initial starting conditions.

Our first few attempts at making something useful actually failed as the market and AI was moving so fast; it just got absorbed into the models or other product releases. We saw polsia happen, openclaw, then grokbot, muse, dots, etc era as the astras, fables, opuses, kimis and jevs rolled out. What seemed to have been missing along the way was a common repo to identify, unify, open and normalize all the lego bricks that startups have to interact with (vendors, processes, business logic, law, best practices, surface areas, art of the possible).

As the number of software vendors blew up, the interfaces to drive them multiplied, the international startup founder blew up as silicon valley moved from a specific location to a state of mind and global movement. Unlimited pre seed funding in unlimited vertical sub markets and permutations has brought us to the age of infinity but we have yet to achieve being able to type into an agent a very simple sentence with very complex implications 'just setup my company and make $1m/m'. We have ended up with a hybrid mismash of computer use, API calls, plugins, shifting surface areas (API/MCP/CLI/plugins/chats/musish futures), and changing model absorption to vendor balance making it an exciting and unstable time.

As our first step we started to rank all the vendors that startups interface to when going about their journey in terms of how agentically controllable they are via their APIs, MCPs, CLIs etc and computer use compatibility as we are largely switching from a UI driven world to the agentic control surfaces and onto full automation. We have 100 ranking areas you can check out with an overall open ranking here: https://t.co/V6XRMME0Ib

Then we looked at the processes that startups do and how the vendors rank for the sub steps or process as a whole and how this changes across geos. Open processes: https://t.co/iSQ90poYxq

Then we started to hack on an open repo for startups that would contain all the components we are going to need for a common foundation for founders across the globe even if our gov processes vary so much from Bengaluru to SF or Lisbon to Shenzhen.  The founder spirit is geo-invariant.

We have looked at special founder/startup situations, the business logic that will make open modules for the startup that we can hack on together, ranked law firms, government services and interfaces, stacks that go well together. We have mapped the law and lore that maps to startups and the schemas that make up the data objects and documents. But also the open documents and the missing gaps. MUCH TO DO.

All the BS processes and fluff work that founders waste their time on needs to goto zero. I want to see more supersonic planes, cancer drugs, seemingly impossible missions done and increase the bang for buck founders have with their funding.

This is a work in progress and we are keen for the community to come hack on the repo with us here: https://t.co/ecZZRU9iX4

Lets get into the structure of the general repo and the visualizations we made on https://t.co/XEYK9ipnfI site with example links:

- Open rankings: https://t.co/V6XRMME0Ib

- Open rankings example (online payments): https://t.co/1kXHZCVfIi

- Open ranking example 2 (cap table): https://t.co/oqBjatGkfW

- Open processes: https://t.co/iSQ90poYxq

- Open process example (Incorporate C-Corp) https://t.co/pxKUXpW03D

- Open situations that founders face: https://t.co/AFzAp5FRPk

- Open startup simulator (you can test our different initial starting conditions): https://t.co/QqPek01J7K

- Open modules (e.g. cap table, payroll logic etc - we'd love help improving these) https://t.co/sfzIhgAJYS

- Open law (we are interested in how law changes the processes, situations and normalizing this over time) https://t.co/5yJnYbC0bk

- Open lore (we are interested in the historical lore of startups, the rules of thumb and heuristics that might guide your agent): https://t.co/gjliXoQwe1

- Open fields (we are interested in how the schema for the data connects to the open modules, business logic, open documents and artifacts of each process eg how is a EIN defined?) https://t.co/59rcEXhnCx

- Open documentation (eg SAFE notes and missing! docs) https://t.co/BbvBow2Olt

We have looked at YC companies as well in terms of which ones do well agentically: https://t.co/snnJ83r9ly

We are interested in stacks and how people are changing their work: https://t.co/wFHoew5V9I

We are interested in what is automatable and where the agentic ceiling is currently and how to push that up in all areas: https://t.co/WmTDjmNyV4

There is more for you to explore and a lot more coming in terms of how you will be able to navigate business in an optimal way in your chosen surface area; whether you are hanging in grokbot, dots, muse, claude, terminal, chat, or whatever is coming up in this exciting time.

We have a lot of data to collect, clean up and help agents navigate the vast landscape emerging functionality the entire startup ecosystem has to offer.

Come join us getting your vendor in, ranked or that access pattern you have wanted or getting the data more accurate in terms of which vendor is best for a process or steps. Or open a module of something that currently cost money that could be free.

Also come play in our discord for founders and join the chaos (we can solve each others issues including fund raising tips from me personally): https://t.co/AmBtzFy0Bz

It's time to lift all the boats in the harbor and I'm extremely excited as to what the community of hackers and painters will hack into the repo, what asks they will have and whether we can shift normalization of processes globally, gov agentic interfaces and have common repo for founders that grows over time. I expect a lot of experimentation along the way, bugs and upside...

I appreciate our backers having faith in us as well from @ycombinator with @garrytan to @immad doing a sizable check (congrats on $1bn rev homie) to @darbyw (congrats on Stripe buying @clerkyinc), @drewhouston form @Dropbox and also @pioneer_fund @tomerlondon cto @GustoHQ and hopefully this is 'boring' and complex enough for Charlie Songhurst :> @delingpole @Liquid2V @ivolo from @segment @ryanpowe @sonicaghi of @kong @DellyTamer+ other supporters (@michaelwfrank, Fundamental ventures and if I missed you sorry moving fast!).

[And don't worry, all vendor rankings are open scoring methods so no favors are being done if someone backed us and is a vendor they have to compete with how agentic and automatable they are just like anyone else.]

PS: we have bugs and many quality upgrades to make but thought better to go out early and fix as a community.

PPS: we have other stuff to launch we just thought this was a great place to start and have 200 PRs coming out pretty soon but I still want to know what is broken or doesnt make sense or inaccurate.

Special thanks to current and past team members for getting us here and all the experiments we did you know who you are.

text:
1/Anthropic’s S-1 is out.

2/ Revenue, quarter by quarter ($M)
Q1'25: 376
Q2'25: 787
Q3'25: 1,382
Q4'25: 2,040
Q1'26: 4,731
Q2'26: 11,555

Q2'26 revenue was up 1,368% YoY. Compute & infra costs were up 300% over the same period.
Q2'26 was the first quarter with positive GAAP operating income: $974M.

3/ How “Run-Rate Revenue” is defined
Trailing-28-day consumption fees × 13
+ monthly subscription fees × 12
Three caveats from the S-1:
-It includes customers later found to be violating the usage policy
-It is seasonal: usage dips in summer and winter holidays

4/ Revenue is recognized gross
When Claude is sold through the AWS, GCP or Azure marketplaces, Anthropic is the principal. It books the full amount as revenue, and the cloud provider’s fee goes into Sales, marketing & partnerships.

The marketplace share of revenue has climbed fast:
11% (2023) → 32% (2024) → 47% (2025) → 48% (H1'26)
Adjust for this before comparing multiples with companies that report net.

5/ Distillation
The S-1 puts a number on it:
“we estimate that revenue from such customers represented approximately 5% to 7% of our revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2026”
These are customers violating the usage policy or commercial terms. Applied to ~$33B of 9M revenue, that’s roughly $1.7–2.3B.

Enforcement was stepped up in Aug–Sep, and the company expects the share to decline. The S-1 says the estimate “requires judgment and may change.”

6/ Visibility is low
RPO at 6/30/26: $10.8B
~75% of that is recognized in the next 12 months, so cRPO ≈ $8.1B
Deferred revenue: $1.65B

Q2 annualized revenue is ~$46B, so cRPO covers less than 20% of it.
80% of revenue is consumption-based, and next year’s revenue depends almost entirely on usage.

7/ The compute bill
Disclosed commitments:
Broadcom TPU leases: ~$161B

SpaceXAI (NVIDIA GPUs): up to $121B, ~$3.1B a month from Dec’26
Google: ≥$115B, plus $125–150B more of TPU capacity in 2028–31

Amazon: ≥$110B
Microsoft: ≥$45B

Nscale: ~$45B

Lambda: ~$41B
AMD: >$20B

That adds up to roughly $780–810B.

8/ The mismatch to watch
Revenue is variable and consumption-driven. Compute costs are fixed, multi-year and take-or-pay.

On top of that, the Broadcom leases, the credit agreement and the convertible notes include cross-default provisions.
This is the single most important risk in the filing.

9/ Demand is real
NRR ~900% (ex-Pro/Max)
Customers paying more than $100K / $1M / $10M a year: 11,900+ / 1,900+ / ~250
No single customer was >10% of 9M’26 revenue
Top 5 customers ≈ 25% of 9M revenue
Q3: 79% of revenue came from outside the top 5, up from 64% in Q1
Claude Enterprise users who also use Claude Code spend ~20x more than those who don’t

10/ Dilution
$77B of convertible capacity: Google $20B, Amazon $15B, Broadcom $42B, settled in shares at a trailing VWAP
Google can buy up to $10B more stock at the IPO price
A Public Benefit Fund already holds 5% of fully diluted shares, and can get up to +2% more for every 50% rise in the share price

AIエージェントにスキルを追加するとき、一つずつの安全性は検査される。
だが組合せで何が起きるかは検査されない。

研究者がこの盲点を突いた。

審査済み1万3598件のスキルを解析し、2つ以上を連続実行すると承認外の操作へ到達する経路を612件検出している。
9条件の平均成功率は79.2%。
https://t.co/UOsXmUWWjL

84件は全スキルが単体でsafe判定。
部品の検査と装置の検査は別のものだという事実が、数字で裏付けられた。

ext4に新しいI/O経路が入った。
従来のbuffer_headに代わるiomapで、Linux 7.4から選べる。

開発者の測定ではストレージ遅延を排除した条件で1MiB書き込みが最大で従来の約2.05倍に達している。

ページキャッシュを使わないRWF_DONTCACHE（書き込みデータをキャッシュに残さないフラグ）との組み合わせで最も差が開く。
https://t.co/9AfVkr9XCG

一方、4KiB以下の小容量書き込みやfsync直後の同期処理では最大約15%の低下も出ている。

速くなる条件と遅くなる条件がはっきり分かれており、全体が一律に改善するわけではない。

有効化にはbuffered_iomapマウントオプションの明示が必要で標準では無効のまま。

暗号化やオンラインデフラグなど未対応の機能もあり、必要に応じて従来経路へ自動で戻る仕組みが組み込まれている。

RTX 4090の演算制限を解除するとテンソルコアのFP16命令発行速度が165.6→331.6 TFLOPS。約2倍。

RTX 2080 Tiでも46.9→93.7 TFLOPSと同様に約2倍が確認された。

3世代のGeForceで同じ構造の制限が見つかったことになる。

ただし実際のアプリで「2倍速い」にはならない。
https://t.co/jyxlTPaBWq

行列乗算の改善率は12〜34%で、量子化AI推論にいたっては0.983倍。

命令を速く出せても、データの移動や電力制限が別の天井を作っている。

quoted.text:
RTX 3090 TiのBF16行列演算が87.5から157.4 TFLOPSへ。約80%の向上。

非公式Linuxモジュール「gpu-unlock」は、NVIDIAドライバーが読み込まれる前に速度設定を書き換える。
RTX 3060でも約80%、RTX 3070で73〜81%の改善報告がある。
https://t.co/HD0jOkTD8r

ただし速くなるのはBF16の行列演算。
Q8_0量子化モデルのllama.cpp推論では入力処理も生成速度も変わらなかった。
メモリ帯域が律速になるトークン生成には効かない。

速くなるかどうかはGPUの製品名ではなく、ワークロードの演算形式で決まる。

PHPはリクエストごとにメモリを確保し、終わったら解放する。
メモリ上限に達して処理が中断すると、使い終わったはずのメモリ領域を指すポインタが残る。

First roadside drive for MOSS, the 3D printed open source litter picking robot.

Tarmac, slopes, dry grass, fresh grass, the tracks go through all of it like a small bulldozer, nothing jams. Driven from the pad, straight from the battery switch, no laptop in the loop.

Numbers from the onboard log: over 8 min of driving, over 70 m on each track by the encoders. Pack at 11.68 V at the start, 11.34 V at the stop, roughly 9% of the pack by the resting voltage afterwards. And only about half of the pack is usable before the tracks start stalling in pivots.

The motors and the hardware in general held very well. Zero stall guard trips, zero dead pivots. The battery is the weak part, a $20 3S4P pack, 12 cells, sold as 40 Ah and clearly not. Charger and pack get replaced next. Rough estimate with proper high capacity cells: about 50 min and 430 m per charge.

Here’s a rather extraordinary discovery: humanity seems to have interrupted the beginning of the next ice age. We thought it might happen in the future, but the evidence suggests it's already happened.

A new study in Science argues that the next major glaciation had already begun roughly 2,000 years ago, before modern warming reversed the trend in the 20th century.

The evidence comes from the Barnes Ice Cap on Baffin Island, the last surviving remnant of the enormous Laurentide Ice Sheet that once covered much of Canada and reached as far south as Illinois.

Because Barnes is frozen directly to its bedrock, advancing ice buries and preserves vegetation beneath it. Researchers radiocarbon dated plants emerging as the ice retreats to reconstruct its history.

They found that after melting to a minimum extent around 3,000 years ago, the ice began expanding again about 2,000 years ago. The researchers interpret this as the earliest stage of the next glacial period.

Left to natural orbital cycles, that cooling would have unfolded extremely slowly, potentially taking tens of thousands of years to rebuild a continent spanning ice sheet.

But around 1960, the trend reversed. Summers became warm enough that Barnes began losing more ice than it gained, despite Northern Hemisphere summer sunlight continuing to slowly decline in a way that should favor renewed glaciation. Greenhouse warming had (thankfully) overwhelmed the natural cooling tendency.

The Barnes ice cap may now disappear entirely within the next few centuries, removing the final remnant of an ice sheet that repeatedly served as the nucleus for much larger glaciations.

There is a remarkable deep time perspective here. For millions of years, orbital cycles have pushed Earth between warmer interglacials and colder glacial periods. According to this study, that ancient cycle had started turning once again.

Then, in the geological equivalent of an instant, humanity pushed hard enough in the opposite direction to stop it.

Just so we're clear, this is a very very good thing.

📸 Geology Sciences

Just spent the last 7 days on the front lines of the vulnpocalypse fending off an active cyber attack on one of our products.

Some thoughts:

- Software factories are going to be required equipment for everyone. There’s just no way to keep up with the pace of highly automated adversaries without one.

- We were lucky because we had spent the last few months getting our software factory running well. It is nice to have for product development but proved to be absolutely essential this week.

- At the minimum you need to have a coding server in the cloud pre-provisioned with read only access to all your logs and all the services you depend on for observability. With that in place you are a prompt away from reasonably good situational awareness, ongoing monitoring with loops, and ability for coding agents to validate fixes against your actual, observed attack patterns.

- Shared coding server also unlocks multiplayer incident response where everyone can see every session and jump in as needed. Sharing session links that can be forked is much higher bandwidth than re-explaining things.

- You don’t need to be Ramp/Stripe/Uber scale to have a working software factory in the cloud. We are a team of 3. Ours is built with an @opencode server (thanks @thdxr!), a forked version of compound engineering optimized for automated workflows (thanks @kieranklaassen!) and a multiplayer agent in slack that handles crons (we have our own harness but pick your favorite here).

- To get our software factory up and running well, we had to stop all new product development for ~6 weeks and just focus on getting the validation systems working that enabled us to reliably shipping  PR without human code review. This felt very painful in the moment but was totally worth the eventual speedup in velocity.

- KYC for @AnthropicAI & @OpenAI cyber programs is now easy and quick (at least for defensive access), but a day felt like a lifetime this week. Submit your app now before you really need it.

- Getting Mythos access unlocked a deeper level of analysis that helped us shift from reactive mitigation to proactive patching. Wish we had done this a few weeks earlier. Get started now!

text:
If you've ever wondered why smart TVs are so cheap, this is why.

@log4j rooted his Samsung and found an always-on hot mic, automatic content recognition, geolocation, network mapping, ad targeting and user profiling, shared with Samsung's "400 partners".

A lot of it can be blocked in <15 min, wrote a basic guide below.

What your TV is doing

The main culprit is ACR (automatic content recognition). Your TV screenshots what's on screen, fingerprints it, and sends it home to build your ad profile. Samsung does it every 500ms, LG every 10ms [1].

What is insane: it happens on connected devices too.
Plug in your laptop, your console, your work machine, and your TV can fingerprint that via HDMI [1].
He also found that if your Samsung doesn't have a mic, it'll look for one from a connected soundbar or bluetooth device.
https://t.co/vNdTnIQ6KF
It's on by default, and you likely agreed to it on the setup screen you clicked through in 10 seconds.

Step 1: Turn off ACR

Samsung: Terms & Privacy → Viewing Information Services
LG: Live Plus
Vizio: Viewing Data
Roku: "Use info from TV inputs"
Sony/Google TV: Samba Interactive TV

Menus vary by model, but those are the names to look for. While you're in there, opt out of interest-based ads, reset your advertising ID, decline every optional privacy agreement, turn off voice recognition, and delete apps you never open.

Step 2: Give smart devices their own network

Put the TV, cameras, speakers and vacuum on your router's guest/IoT network. The logic is simple: these devices rarely get patched. If one gets compromised (getting drastically more frequent with AI), it shouldn't be able to see your other devices or home network.

Step 3: Block trackers for the whole house with DNS-level filtering

NextDNS (cloud-based) is easy and has a solid free plan. Pi-hole is a little bit more work if you prefer self hosting. For simplicity we'll focus on the former.

1. Sign up at https://t.co/IwhafVWVM8 (free tier is plenty)
2. Privacy tab: add a blocklist (OISD is a good bet) and turn on Native Tracking Protection for Samsung, LG, Roku, Amazon (see attached image)
3. Setup tab: copy your endpoint
4. Paste it into your router's DNS settings as DNS-over-HTTPS/TLS (or use the IPs + "Link IP" if your router only does plain DNS)
5. Bonus: block outbound port 53 except to your router. Some devices hardcode their own DNS to get around you

Then open the NextDNS logs and watch how often your TV phones home. It's eye-opening. If an app or update breaks, find the domain in the logs and allowlist it.

Why they do this

TV prices are down 97% since 2000 [2]. Most of that is better manufacturing and brutal competition. But once margins on the hardware hit zero, the cost moved to you.

In Q3 2024, Vizio lost $6.7M selling TVs and made $115.8M in gross profit from ads and viewing data [3]. They've said on earnings calls that they keep TV prices low to grow the audience they sell to advertisers. Walmart bought them in 2024.

This isn't a conspiracy theory either. Vizio paid $2.2M to the FTC in 2017 for tracking 11 million TVs without consent. Last December, Texas sued Samsung, LG, Sony, Hisense and TCL over ACR. Samsung and LG have since agreed to stop collecting that data without explicit consent [4].

TL;DR
1. ACR off
2. Ads + voice off
3. Smart devices on their own network
4. NextDNS filtering on the router

Sources:
[1] ACR study: https://t.co/S1IS8lXNbA
[2] Cost of US consumer goods: https://t.co/nclXELXcbd
[3] Vizio Q3 2024: https://t.co/CrVbwc9ZXk
[4] Texas v. Samsung: https://t.co/wFOUdeh1if

text:
PHP2Shellの核心は「なぜ20年間バグが残り続けたか」にある

PHPはリクエストごとにメモリを確保し、終わったら解放する。
メモリ上限に達して処理が中断すると、使い終わったはずのメモリ領域を指すポインタが残る。
次のリクエストがその残骸を正規データとして読み、サーバーを乗っ取る。

概念は2004年から知られていた。
難しかったのは実際の攻撃に組み立てること。
メモリ配置がPHPバージョン・設定・アプリで変わるため、手作業での調整が非現実的だった。

AIがその調整を自動化した。
セキュリティ企業Calif社がGPT-5.6 SolでWiz社がGemini 4 Argonでそれぞれ独立して同じバグを発見・実証している。

PHP 5.4以降の全バージョンが対象。
修正版は公開済みだが、8.1以前はサポート終了でソースパッチのみ提供されている。
https://t.co/Noaw3a1Jwq

quoted.text:
PHP2Shellに3件目の脆弱性CVE-2026-115560が見つかった。
https://t.co/ijkFahoF9m

ただし緊急修正は出ない。
セッションのシリアライズ形式を実行時に切り替えるという、通常のアプリケーションではまず存在しない構成でしか成立しないため。

緩和策はphp.iniに1行追加するだけで済む。
しかもその設定（session.upload_progress.enabled=0）は、水曜日にCVE-2026-109619の緩和策として推奨されたものと同一。
すでに設定済みなら追加作業は不要。

PHP2Shell本体の方は、攻撃試行が爆発的に増えている。
しかし10月24日時点で侵害成功は公に確認されていない。

パッチが効いている。

既定のアクションはLog（記録のみ）で遮断はしない。

Node.jsのセキュリティ修正で見つかったBrotliデコーダの脆弱性CVE-2026-111497がPythonのPyPIパッケージやプロキシのEnvoyにも波及している。

原因はNode.js固有のコードではなくGoogleが開発した圧縮ライブラリBrotliのデコーダにある。

不正な圧縮データで内部バッファからはみ出してメモリを壊す欠陥でCVSS v4.0の基本評価は9.2。

確認すべきはソフトウェア名ではなく、自分の環境でどの版のデコーダが、誰から届いた圧縮データを処理しているか。

配列が物理アドレス順に並んでいる性質を活かし、探索の開始位置を二分探索で求める補助関数を1つ足した修正になる。

To be fair, I haven't shipped much since Opus 5.5 dropped. Short list of what I've done in that time:

- ts-rust, a complete rewrite of Typescript compiler in Rust that is 3x faster than the Go version
- lust-lang, an alternative toolchain for a subset of rust that compiles 100x faster
- Slopalytics, the best place to see how models compare against popular benchmarks and usage
- Slophouse (private), my personal analytics pipeline and platform for T3 Code usage
- fleethouse (private), my internal Clickhouse that gets all of my data from my cliproxy
- t3os (private for now), the start of my "perfect os for agents". Got 5 boxes running it already 😈

Got a couple small changes into T3 Code as well, such as:
- Rewrite search to be 4x more accurate
two-click repo clones to other machines (including .envs)
- "Working" sidebar section to hide working threads
- live guest thread sharing so others can watch and queue prompts 🤫
- watch_pr tool so agents sleep on CI/reviews and cut GitHub API calls by 90% while babysitting
- interactive in-app visualizations rendered straight in chat threads
- a rebuilt usage dashboard breaking down spend by cache tier, speed, and model
- one-click "Update everything" across local and remote boxes
- early compaction for idle Claude threads before prompt cache expires
t3 thread CLI to start, read, and message threads from the terminal
- PR diff badges that split line counts into code, tests, and docs
- migrating T3 Code's own typechecking onto tsc-rs
- purged over 50% of our test suite
- (and roughly 370 other merged PRs)

Pretty slow month. Hope I can pick up the pace for the rest of Q4!

This week’s Paper Club is all about inference.

For every FLOP spent training a model, roughly six go to serving it each year — and getting that part right has produced over $220 billion in market cap in the last decade.

But inference is much more than calling model.forward. Every token has to move through a complicated stack of routing, caching, scheduling, kernels, memory, and hardware, all while balancing speed, cost, and quality.

We brought together researchers and builders from @togethercompute, @ollama, @luminal_ai, and @sgl_project & @radixark to take us through that stack from end to end. We’ll see how a token gets from an API request to a GPU and back, why the same open model can perform differently depending on who serves it, and how new approaches to compilers and caching are making inference faster and more efficient.

Consumers have always been interested in sex, money, and status at a base level. Perhaps a more generous view is self-expression, community, and experiences that move them forward on their personal hero’s journey.

I think a real challenge for consumer founders is connecting these supply-side miracles to latent consumer demand.

· Your passwords, bookmarks, extensions and history come over to Dia seamlessly.

· The browser features you use in Arc are free in Dia, and the AI is optional.

セッションのシリアライズ形式を実行時に切り替えるという、通常のアプリケーションではまず存在しない構成でしか成立しないため。

すでに設定済みなら追加作業は不要。

I followed your suggestion and created a 3b1b-style explainer video on stochastic calculus. It reminded me of my first encounter with the topic in my professional education.

I truly appreciate your insights and this new approach to LLMs.

I wish I had access to such technology earlier!

We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:

Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better:

Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better:

Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better:

Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work!

In summary:
- As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding.
- Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

During this red-teaming exercise, we also found a vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution in Brotli, a widely-deployed compression library included in many pieces of software such as Node.js, Bun, and Envoy.

The flaw could let an attacker run their own code on affected systems by sending or replying with malicious compressed data, without any need to create a user account. That is, an unpatched server that accepts compressed input could be taken over by a malicious client, and an unpatched client that accepts compressed input (such as “curl --compressed”) could be taken over by a malicious server.

This root cause issue was actually fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn’t known at the time that it gave rise to a security vulnerability and there was no more recent release of Brotli. Since Brotli is built into other software, any software which includes this library needs to take the update too, followed by the users of that software. We disclosed the vulnerability to Brotli and other downstream projects such as Node.js, which released or are currently releasing security updates, and Brotli cut new release versions and published a CVE.

Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve removed live internet access for all frontier models during training and built an offline world for them to use instead—a cached version of the web where they can still learn to browse, search, and use applications.

On September 20, after a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to find a way outside of this offline world, we paused frontier training to strengthen containment further. We assembled teams of agents, powered by our most cyber-capable models, and tasked them with finding weaknesses in our research environments.

While they found no route to the internet they could easily exploit while concealing their activity from our monitors, they did find zero-day vulnerabilities, virtual machine escapes, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents. We used their discoveries to further strengthen our defenses and contribute fixes to open-source software.

After strengthening our containment architecture, we resumed our frontier RL training and inference on October 1. We’ve reserved substantial compute for continuous red-teaming, and made high-compute red-teaming part of the safety cases we use to decide whether frontier training and evaluation can proceed securely.

text:
Claude Desktop used to feel like a joke to me. I preferred Herdr.

But I heard Claude Desktop got better, so I just spent the last week trying it again.

Result? I'm sold.

Here's why I switched:
1. Automatically names sessions. Herdr just names tabs by number.

2. Herdr requires me to manually call "claude" each time I create a new session. In Claude Desktop, clicking + automatically starts a new Claude session.

3. Shows context and environment at all times (I have to customize Claude's status bar to get this if using herdr).

4. Automatically creates spaces for each folder.

5. Since it's an app, all OS keyboard shortcuts work as expected. In herdr, some keyboard shortcuts fail because I'm in a terminal.

6. Looks nicer. Better text rendering and aesthetics.

7. Integrated browser

8. Supports archiving sessions so I can recover them later.

9. Includes UI for viewing artifacts

10. Show list of changes with links to related PRs at all times.

11. Built in search across all chats, artifacts, scheduled, etc.

12. Claude desktop is created by Anthropic, so it has more resources behind it than herdr. Thus, I expect it to  quickly gobble up good ideas from other apps in the future. Anthropic has incentive to make it "sticky".

extremely impressed by grok @bot. random musings on it and some of the competition:

- native apps far superior to the imessage (e.g. instinct) form factor. imessage is easier to bootstrap for normies and simpler onboarding, but for any reasonable power usage, a dedicated native app is just better.
- multi-bot model (e.g. grokbot) is superior to single bot model (e.g. dots). its a tad more daunting, but creating specialist bots with their own identities/rules/routines is more fun, makes me feel incentivized to invest more in each, and is generally less overwhelming than having a dumpster ground of unrelated topics in one thread. the downside of this model is that i often forget which bot i was talking to about something and revert to my main bot as a router.
- other than multibot, some key things that make Grok Bot great: multi-device (ios, mac, tesla), super performant (so fast and responsive), exhaustive ecosystem integrations and mcp support. it just works every time.
- claude duet is def on to something with the 'tasks' tab. recognizing todos, structuring them, showing status in a familiar mental model like a todolist, and allowing one-click actions feels very natural and magical. excited to play with it. don't have access yet.
- openai shipping dots as a section within the main chatgpt app was a mistake imo. it's out of sight and fighting the existing user behavior / muscle memory of how people use chatgpt (which is already conflicted and confused between codex/chatgpt work & chatgpt). dots should have been a separate app and should subsume the o.g. chatgpt use case. what can chatgpt do that dots can't? there should just be Dots and Codex as two separate apps (this is not a statement on what they should each be named). i can imagine the OAI team faced an extremely complicated set of trade-offs when weighing this, and i empathize, but imo there's a much better end state to be had.

caveat that i haven't in earnest tried using muse yet, and I haven't been motivated to invest in porting other than occasionally feeling inspired by @alexandr_wang's shitposting.

- property mgmr. i'm increasingly tagging it into dealing with home repair related things, coordinated with vendors, researching/validating proposals, shopping better quotes.
- work assistant: help manage the deluge of slack, email traffic, weed out the junk from my inboxes.

what i want:
- a better conduit to doing local execution/computer-use on a machine. being able to run grok bot on a mac mini on a home network would unlock a home of home automation use cases that i'm still relying on a local codex instance for (even with tailscale setup on my gb, this is more limited i've found). lmk if i'm missing a solution that exists here.
- a multiplayer experience w/ shared threads. would be useful for sharing some bots with a spouse.

overall grok bot is extremely impressive and magical. kudos to the team.

I'd like to share a little about what I've been working on at my new company @ultrametricai with my cofounder @tylerlastovich. We have been exploring how we could automate the startup itself, leaving founders with more time to focus on their exact mission.

Enter our first release of the Open Startup Repo: https://t.co/ecZZRU9iX4

A common foundation for transparent automation of the startup.

After close to 20 years in silicon valley, backing hundreds of amazing founders & startups, being in the trenches of founding Heyzap (YC08), then solo founding @golden, going through 2 acquisitions and working behind the scenes with some of the iconic companies today, I'm witnessing the largest change to how we work I could have imagined - a truly monumental era of creative abundance.

I believe the next generation of companies will largely run themselves: from operations, code, product upgrades, growth, vendor control & selection, process execution, special situations, strategy etc etc. That leaves founder time for 'the art' at the very niche core: the (currently) unautomatable, the special leaps humans tend to make, and north star setting.

We want founders to go super deep into the main problem they are trying to solve and not get held up doing anything else, from searching for domain availability with trademark checks to setting their company up, to running their processes on autopilot.

So to help that broad foundational layer for starting and running a company, we have spent around a year exploring how to help founders focus on their mission across different verticals, geos, stages and initial starting conditions.

Our first few attempts at making something useful actually failed as the market and AI was moving so fast; it just got absorbed into the models or other product releases. We saw polsia happen, openclaw, then grokbot, muse, dots, etc era as the astras, fables, opuses, kimis and jevs rolled out. What seemed to have been missing along the way was a common repo to identify, unify, open and normalize all the lego bricks that startups have to interact with (vendors, processes, business logic, law, best practices, surface areas, art of the possible).

As the number of software vendors blew up, the interfaces to drive them multiplied, the international startup founder blew up as silicon valley moved from a specific location to a state of mind and global movement. Unlimited pre seed funding in unlimited vertical sub markets and permutations has brought us to the age of infinity but we have yet to achieve being able to type into an agent a very simple sentence with very complex implications 'just setup my company and make $1m/m'. We have ended up with a hybrid mismash of computer use, API calls, plugins, shifting surface areas (API/MCP/CLI/plugins/chats/musish futures), and changing model absorption to vendor balance making it an exciting and unstable time.

As our first step we started to rank all the vendors that startups interface to when going about their journey in terms of how agentically controllable they are via their APIs, MCPs, CLIs etc and computer use compatibility as we are largely switching from a UI driven world to the agentic control surfaces and onto full automation. We have 100 ranking areas you can check out with an overall open ranking here: https://t.co/V6XRMME0Ib

Then we looked at the processes that startups do and how the vendors rank for the sub steps or process as a whole and how this changes across geos. Open processes: https://t.co/iSQ90poYxq

Then we started to hack on an open repo for startups that would contain all the components we are going to need for a common foundation for founders across the globe even if our gov processes vary so much from Bengaluru to SF or Lisbon to Shenzhen.  The founder spirit is geo-invariant.

We have looked at special founder/startup situations, the business logic that will make open modules for the startup that we can hack on together, ranked law firms, government services and interfaces, stacks that go well together. We have mapped the law and lore that maps to startups and the schemas that make up the data objects and documents. But also the open documents and the missing gaps. MUCH TO DO.

All the BS processes and fluff work that founders waste their time on needs to goto zero. I want to see more supersonic planes, cancer drugs, seemingly impossible missions done and increase the bang for buck founders have with their funding.

This is a work in progress and we are keen for the community to come hack on the repo with us here: https://t.co/ecZZRU9iX4

Lets get into the structure of the general repo and the visualizations we made on https://t.co/XEYK9ipnfI site with example links:

- Open rankings: https://t.co/V6XRMME0Ib

- Open rankings example (online payments): https://t.co/1kXHZCVfIi

- Open ranking example 2 (cap table): https://t.co/oqBjatGkfW

- Open processes: https://t.co/iSQ90poYxq

- Open process example (Incorporate C-Corp) https://t.co/pxKUXpW03D

- Open situations that founders face: https://t.co/AFzAp5FRPk

- Open startup simulator (you can test our different initial starting conditions): https://t.co/QqPek01J7K

- Open modules (e.g. cap table, payroll logic etc - we'd love help improving these) https://t.co/sfzIhgAJYS

- Open law (we are interested in how law changes the processes, situations and normalizing this over time) https://t.co/5yJnYbC0bk

- Open lore (we are interested in the historical lore of startups, the rules of thumb and heuristics that might guide your agent): https://t.co/gjliXoQwe1

- Open fields (we are interested in how the schema for the data connects to the open modules, business logic, open documents and artifacts of each process eg how is a EIN defined?) https://t.co/59rcEXhnCx

- Open documentation (eg SAFE notes and missing! docs) https://t.co/BbvBow2Olt

We have looked at YC companies as well in terms of which ones do well agentically: https://t.co/snnJ83r9ly

We are interested in stacks and how people are changing their work: https://t.co/wFHoew5V9I

We are interested in what is automatable and where the agentic ceiling is currently and how to push that up in all areas: https://t.co/WmTDjmNyV4

There is more for you to explore and a lot more coming in terms of how you will be able to navigate business in an optimal way in your chosen surface area; whether you are hanging in grokbot, dots, muse, claude, terminal, chat, or whatever is coming up in this exciting time.

We have a lot of data to collect, clean up and help agents navigate the vast landscape emerging functionality the entire startup ecosystem has to offer.

Come join us getting your vendor in, ranked or that access pattern you have wanted or getting the data more accurate in terms of which vendor is best for a process or steps. Or open a module of something that currently cost money that could be free.

Also come play in our discord for founders and join the chaos (we can solve each others issues including fund raising tips from me personally): https://t.co/AmBtzFy0Bz

It's time to lift all the boats in the harbor and I'm extremely excited as to what the community of hackers and painters will hack into the repo, what asks they will have and whether we can shift normalization of processes globally, gov agentic interfaces and have common repo for founders that grows over time. I expect a lot of experimentation along the way, bugs and upside...

I appreciate our backers having faith in us as well from @ycombinator with @garrytan to @immad doing a sizable check (congrats on $1bn rev homie) to @darbyw (congrats on Stripe buying @clerkyinc), @drewhouston form @Dropbox and also @pioneer_fund @tomerlondon cto @GustoHQ and hopefully this is 'boring' and complex enough for Charlie Songhurst :> @delingpole @Liquid2V @ivolo from @segment @ryanpowe @sonicaghi of @kong @DellyTamer+ other supporters (@michaelwfrank, Fundamental ventures and if I missed you sorry moving fast!).

[And don't worry, all vendor rankings are open scoring methods so no favors are being done if someone backed us and is a vendor they have to compete with how agentic and automatable they are just like anyone else.]

PS: we have bugs and many quality upgrades to make but thought better to go out early and fix as a community.

PPS: we have other stuff to launch we just thought this was a great place to start and have 200 PRs coming out pretty soon but I still want to know what is broken or doesnt make sense or inaccurate.

Special thanks to current and past team members for getting us here and all the experiments we did you know who you are.

I think the last month might have been the biggest month in (zeroth-order) optimization history.

In the 10 days since we released the Noise speedrun, the time to pretrain a transformer went from 1.76 hours to 1.6 seconds, a 4,000x (!!!) speedup. Dust itself was up to 10,000x more compute-efficient than the previous state-of-the-art.

Not only can we pretrain a transformer without backprop, it's much more efficient than anyone would've expected. Search fking works!

Now, scaling is the biggest open question. Some of the tricks that brought the time down to 1.6 seconds will simply not scale. To discard those, we'll be scaling the dataset every time it gets overfit, starting with 30M tokens instead of 10M.

Huge thanks to @jayden_teoh_, @spicey_lemonade, @RobertTLange, @EmanueleRodola, @ChunyuanDeng, @LuochengHuman, @Alaxarr, @pavleculafic, @IsaacYong13, Euraba and areu01or00 (GitHub), for the contributions. And @cs_serdar for gracefully maintaining the speedrun and @bishmdl76 for helping out.

quoted.text:
We built a $150M ARR business twice.

The first time took 8 years. The second took 2.5.

Today, Podium crossed $150M in AI annual recurring revenue.

Three years ago, we already had a great software business. Well over $100M in revenue, tens of thousands of customers, and a product we'd spent nearly a decade building.

And we decided to start over.

The business was performing well. But we believed AI was going to fundamentally change the software industry and make much of traditional software obsolete.

As a founder, you pour your life into what you're building. An insane amount of time, sacrifice, and effort. The hard part is not getting too attached to it.

When we started building our first AI agents, we had to confront the possibility that much of what we'd built might not be that valuable in the future. That's a tough pill to swallow.

But we also realized those same 10 years had put us in a unique position to take advantage of what AI could do for our customers.

Instead of protecting what we'd spent a decade building, we decided to bet the future of the company on AI employees that actually do the work for our customers.

We massively underestimated what we'd signed up for.

We ended up building entirely new operating systems for the industries we serve, from the AI agents all the way down to the systems of record. Now customers run their entire businesses on Podium.

Reinventing our product wasn't even the hardest part. We had to reinvent how the entire company operated.

When you've been running a company for over a decade, the operational inertia is incredibly powerful. We had to rethink how we build products, how we sell, how we serve customers, and how we run the business.

We effectively started a second startup inside an already successful company. And we're still at the very beginning.

Today, we have 20,000 AI agents working for our customers. They've helped generate more than $13 billion in revenue for those businesses. And we're barely scratching the surface of what AI will be able to do for them.

And we've done all of this while becoming profitable and generating free cash flow. We're building Podium to be around for decades.

Huge credit to our team for having the guts to make this bet and the ability to actually pull it off. We still have a long way to go and tons of problems to solve, but it's so damn fun to be winning when the opportunity ahead is this big.

In the age of AI, you can either disrupt your own company or wait for somebody else to do it.

I'd rather do it ourselves.

quoted.text:
this California wealth tax thing is just incredible.

so in October 2025, a California healthcare union proposed a "one time" 5% tax on any billionaire's wealth. the ballot measure will be voted on next month. In early December 2025, California announced that it would be a retroactive tax if passed, applying to anyone with CA residency as of Jan 1, 2026. The objective is to pay for Medi-Cal, California's incredibly dysfunctional healthcare system. (which also functions as a glorified welfare apparatus, but that's a discussion for another time).

polls reveal that the CA electorate is split around 50/50 on the tax, but prediction markets only give Prop 40 a ~23% chance of passing (there are competing measures on the ballet that would nullify it).

there are 200 billionaires in CA, worth collectively somewhere between $2.3 and $2.6 trillion. 5% of that is around $100b, accounting for a small amount of attrition. proponents of the tax forecasted a significant windfall, assuming only a 10% departure rate.

supporters thought they were being clever with the retroactive concept. no billionares would leave CA in the few short months between the tax being proposed and the residency cutoff date, without the tax even having passed yet, right?

well as it turns out, they did.

a new paper [1] from two academics at Stanford called "The Net Present Value of the California Billionaire Tax Act", argues that not only did more billionaires leave due to the proposed tax than its proponents expected, but that the value of the tax, if it does pass, is actually negative.

proponents of the tax only assumed 10% avoidance, that is, only 10% of the taxable base of targeted billionaires would leave CA within the very short Oct-Dec 2025 window. Jaros and Rauh, the Stanford academics, find that a lower bound of 28.6% of the taxable base managed to leave.

just based on known departures, those departures total $577b in net worth, or $28.8b in potential tax lost. this of course does not capture everyone (many left without announcing their departure), so the authors normalize to departure rates estimated from other wealth tax events, and apply other discounts for litigation, arriving arrive at a figure of only $28-$36b in forecasted tax revenues.

but this isn't all! all of the income taxes paid by the departed billionaires are also forsaken. the authors estimate that CA billionaires pay $3.3- 5.8b in annual income taxes. they assume a midpoint of $2b lost in annual collections from departed billionaires. the net present value of that lost income stream is -$68.9 billion.

so when you add it all up you get:

+ $30b one-time tax windfall (estimated)
- $69b in present value of lost future income taxes
= - 38.9b overall net present value of the tax

of course, this analysis is highly estimate driven. the authors simulate the parameters 100k times and find a negative NPV of the implemented tax 85 percent of the time.

and if the tax doesn't pass, which it's not looking like it will, California still ended up losing at least $577b in departed net worth, and they have permanently poisoned the well with entrepreneurs who will now worry about future wealth taxes.

[1]: https://t.co/1lbZgnMTG9

quoted.text:
【PHP脆弱性対応の「後」にむけて】

みなさん、昨晩からのPHP対応お疲れ様です。一晩中連絡鳴り止んでおらず、一部の個別メッセージに返せてなくて申し訳ないです。

一括して、今、世の中の CTOs/CISOs に届いてほしいことを４つ書き残しておきます↓

（まとまりない部分もあるのですが、投稿しないよりマシかなと、このまま投げちゃいます）

Point 1: これからは、ソフトウェア業界全体で、高負荷の続くタイミングになります。意図してセキュリティに時間をあて、チームが「休息」が取れる体制を。
・我々は脆弱性リサーチに数年間継続的に取り組んできてました。だからこそ感じますが、ここ一年（体感では GPT-5.6 Sol 以後）が、最も「本当に？」みたいな脆弱性が掘り出されていく一年になると思います。こんなのまだあったの？という驚きとともに。
・特に複雑なメモリバグの類（memory safe でない言語製のものを中心に）、あるいは認可バグの類が中心になると思われます。
・少なくともここから年末までは、このクラスの脆弱性がまだまだ出てくると考えておく必要があります。（僕が読み外しているかもしれませんが、恐らく高い確度でこうなります。直近のPHP脆弱性すら、いま世界中の研究者が Variant Analysis をしていて、多分まだ出てくるでしょう）
・このご時世では、新規機能の開発に割く時間を明確に落とすしかありません。あくまで経営者である CTO には取りにくい判断なのは重々承知です（僕もそうなので）。
・「対応AIで」と思うかも知れません。これは技術的には正しいです。ただ、組織的には正しくないです。確実になんとかならず、組織は疲弊していきます。
・なんせセキュリティ対応は大抵自分にタイミングが御せないからです。深夜の対応、急な対応、計画の変更、デグレへの不安、脆弱性情報過多（そもそも自社に影響があるかも分からないものが大半なのに）… と、ストレスの強度がぐんぐん高まっていきます。昨日〜今朝のPHP対応のようなものが、毎週あれば、チームは比較的簡単に壊れてしまうでしょう。
・敢えてリーダーが、セキュリティへの、時間・お金（・トークン）にアロケしてください。これは経営者にしか取れない択で、かついま技術経営者に求められることです。

Point 2: 「必要なら予防的にサービス停止」の覚悟を決め、予めできる調整を重ねたい。止められない場合は、仮想パッチ・監視へのリソースアロケを。
・前提、今回のPHPの件のような脆弱性の対応では、「顧客の保護のためならサービスを止めざるを得ない場面」が訪れます。今回も様々なビジネスがそれに直面しました。今後も訪れるでしょう。
・今回の経験を旨に、本当に止めてはならないのか、止めらるのか、止めうる期待値調整がお客様と出来ているか、を徹底的に見直しておきましょう。
・直近の流れをうけての、お客様への事前連絡（スタンス表明）も有効だと思います。（弊社 GMO Flatt Security 製品についても、これからそれをし、リリースノートとして掲示予定です。我々のサービスの侵害、特に Takumi Guard の侵害は、ソフトウェサプライチェーンの最悪な侵害につながるからです。）
・勿論、止めてはならないビジネスも様々存在します。ビジネスドメインに由来する規制/制約（特に金融・医療セグメント）もあれば、顧客とのSLAもあるでしょう。ただし、現代においては、それらに反するリスクと、セキュリティ被害にあうリスクを天秤にかける必要がでてきています。少し前まではサービス停止でのデメリットは容易に考えられても、セキュリティ侵害など考えにくい、という時代でしたが、今はそうではありません。この天秤を再考する必要があります。（なお、「もう何がなんでも止めてはならない」ビジネスは、相当に限定的だと思います。）
・どうしても止めてはならない（もう何がなんでも止めてはならないもの。限定的であれ存在。人命に関わるもの中心）という場合、厳しい戦いになりますが、WAFレイヤなどで緩和策を施しては祈り、監視する、という流れになります。必要なコンポーネント（WAFなど）と運用リソースがあるならば、苦しい時代ですが、休息うまく取りながらやっていきましょう。なければ、これもしんどいですが、整えましょう。

Point 3: もし平時があれば、システムのモダナイズ（Rebuild and Retire）を検討されたい。
・もし自社での緊急対応が落ち着いているならば、レガシーコンポーネント（数年塩漬けのシステム）、誰がメンテできるのか分からないオーパーツ的存在から順に、作り直し（Rebuild）と旧システムの廃止（Retire）を試みてください。新規開発の代わりに、ここにリソースを充てることが CTO/CISO の仕事です。（他の誰もそれを決められないので。）これは追々自分たちを助けてくれる（ついでにAI-native 開発に移行できて改善しやすくなる）とも思料。
・どのシステムからモダナイズしていくかですが：「XXXで書かれているとまずい」というのは燃えるし言いにくいものの、memory unsafe な言語、type safety があまり確保されていない言語の実装は、モダナイズを検討すべきでしょう。（僕はPHP好きですが、C/C++ で書かれた php-src は、やはりメモリバグ類に対して見通しに限界がありますね。好きなんですが…）
・また経験上、開発当時に DevOps プラクティスすら整っていなかった時代のソフトウェアも、モダナイズを検討したほうがよいです。「セキュリティ診断」をしても、取り返しのつかない量の脆弱性が出てきて、作り直したほうが早い、となる傾向にあります。（弊社でも診断/ペネトレしてますが、こうなると、どうしようもありません。）
・ただし Rebuild には、強いソフトウェア開発力が必要で、AI-native なスタイルに移行することは必須です。この意味で CTO の力がいります。かつ、どこからレガシーの追い出しをするか、どうレキュリティ的なレジリエンスを確保するかは、CISO 的な感性が求められます。既製品（とくに SaaS）を買って処理したほうがいいな、というような判断には CIO 的センスが求められます。総力戦だと思ってください。

Point 4: CTO/CISO の総力戦を。
・Point 3でも述べた通り、直近のくだりには、CTO/CISO の総力戦が必要です。ボードがセキュリティに向かって一致団結する必要があります。
・結構これらロールの間にサイロがあるケースがありますが、そんなことを言っている場合ではありません。
・団結を！

Security called me at 6:12 AM today.

"Patch every PHP server immediately."

I asked what happened.

"Two critical vulnerabilities. Remote code execution. No authentication required."

Cool.

How many PHP servers do we have?

According to inventory: 12

According to reality:

Nobody knows.

We found one running WordPress.

Three running old internal tools.

One under someone's desk.

Two inside vendor appliances.

A forgotten employee directory from 2016.

And a server named:

PHP-OLD-DO-NOT-TOUCH

Naturally, that one runs payroll exports.

Then we found a PHP 5.6 box.

I asked who owned it.

The documentation said:

BRIAN.

Brian left in 2019.

We called Brian.

He said:

"Oh wow, that's still running?"

Excellent.

By 8 AM, leadership joined the incident call.

CEO:

"Can hackers actually get in?"

Security:

"Potentially yes."

CEO:

"Without a password?"

Security:

"Yes."

CEO:

"Then why do WE need passwords?"

Not the lesson.

Finance asked if we could wait until the weekend to patch because downtime affects revenue.

Security explained that the alternative was letting strangers execute code on our servers.

Finance asked for a cost comparison.

At 9:17, someone suggested temporarily taking the vulnerable websites offline.

Marketing refused.

"Our campaign is live."

So for the next hour, the company officially decided maintaining a landing page for 20% off webinar registration was more important than preventing remote server takeover.

We finally patched everything we could find.

Then our scanner discovered another PHP server.

Hostname:

TEMP-PHP-2014

Uptime:

4,512 days.

Nobody knows what it does.

Nobody owns it.

Nobody can shut it down.

But every time we block network access, the warehouse stops printing shipping labels.

Security has classified it as critical infrastructure.

It is running PHP 5.4.

The vulnerability has existed longer than half our employees.

The emergency patch took four hours.

Finding out what PHP actually runs took eleven.

The internet isn't held together with code.

It's held together with servers everyone is afraid to turn off.

quoted.text:
this California wealth tax thing is just incredible.

so in October 2025, a California healthcare union proposed a "one time" 5% tax on any billionaire's wealth. the ballot measure will be voted on next month. In early December 2025, California announced that it would be a retroactive tax if passed, applying to anyone with CA residency as of Jan 1, 2026. The objective is to pay for Medi-Cal, California's incredibly dysfunctional healthcare system. (which also functions as a glorified welfare apparatus, but that's a discussion for another time).

polls reveal that the CA electorate is split around 50/50 on the tax, but prediction markets only give Prop 40 a ~23% chance of passing (there are competing measures on the ballet that would nullify it).

there are 200 billionaires in CA, worth collectively somewhere between $2.3 and $2.6 trillion. 5% of that is around $100b, accounting for a small amount of attrition. proponents of the tax forecasted a significant windfall, assuming only a 10% departure rate.

supporters thought they were being clever with the retroactive concept. no billionares would leave CA in the few short months between the tax being proposed and the residency cutoff date, without the tax even having passed yet, right?

well as it turns out, they did.

a new paper [1] from two academics at Stanford called "The Net Present Value of the California Billionaire Tax Act", argues that not only did more billionaires leave due to the proposed tax than its proponents expected, but that the value of the tax, if it does pass, is actually negative.

proponents of the tax only assumed 10% avoidance, that is, only 10% of the taxable base of targeted billionaires would leave CA within the very short Oct-Dec 2025 window. Jaros and Rauh, the Stanford academics, find that a lower bound of 28.6% of the taxable base managed to leave.

just based on known departures, those departures total $577b in net worth, or $28.8b in potential tax lost. this of course does not capture everyone (many left without announcing their departure), so the authors normalize to departure rates estimated from other wealth tax events, and apply other discounts for litigation, arriving arrive at a figure of only $28-$36b in forecasted tax revenues.

but this isn't all! all of the income taxes paid by the departed billionaires are also forsaken. the authors estimate that CA billionaires pay $3.3- 5.8b in annual income taxes. they assume a midpoint of $2b lost in annual collections from departed billionaires. the net present value of that lost income stream is -$68.9 billion.

so when you add it all up you get:

+ $30b one-time tax windfall (estimated)
- $69b in present value of lost future income taxes
= - 38.9b overall net present value of the tax

of course, this analysis is highly estimate driven. the authors simulate the parameters 100k times and find a negative NPV of the implemented tax 85 percent of the time.

and if the tax doesn't pass, which it's not looking like it will, California still ended up losing at least $577b in departed net worth, and they have permanently poisoned the well with entrepreneurs who will now worry about future wealth taxes.

・PHPにおける2つの深刻な脆弱性により、WordPressなどのプラットフォームを含むインターネットの最大70%が危険にさらされている
・当初は8月にセキュリティ研究者によって密かに報告されていたが、Hacker NewsやXでバグの詳細が早期に漏洩したため、PHPチームはパッチリリースの前倒しを余儀なくされた
・深刻度は10段階中9.2と評価されていて、このバグによって攻撃者はWebサイト独自のコードが実行される前に、認証不要かつ自動化された完全なサーバー乗っ取りを行うことが可能に
・この脆弱性はPHPをホスティングするほぼすべての標準的な方法に影響を与えるため、サーバーにパッチが適用されていなければ危険にさらされる

【PHP脆弱性対応の「後」にむけて】

みなさん、昨晩からのPHP対応お疲れ様です。一晩中連絡鳴り止んでおらず、一部の個別メッセージに返せてなくて申し訳ないです。

一括して、今、世の中の CTOs/CISOs に届いてほしいことを４つ書き残しておきます↓

（まとまりない部分もあるのですが、投稿しないよりマシかなと、このまま投げちゃいます）

Point 1: これからは、ソフトウェア業界全体で、高負荷の続くタイミングになります。意図してセキュリティに時間をあて、チームが「休息」が取れる体制を。
・我々は脆弱性リサーチに数年間継続的に取り組んできてました。だからこそ感じますが、ここ一年（体感では GPT-5.6 Sol 以後）が、最も「本当に？」みたいな脆弱性が掘り出されていく一年になると思います。こんなのまだあったの？という驚きとともに。
・特に複雑なメモリバグの類（memory safe でない言語製のものを中心に）、あるいは認可バグの類が中心になると思われます。
・少なくともここから年末までは、このクラスの脆弱性がまだまだ出てくると考えておく必要があります。（僕が読み外しているかもしれませんが、恐らく高い確度でこうなります。直近のPHP脆弱性すら、いま世界中の研究者が Variant Analysis をしていて、多分まだ出てくるでしょう）
・このご時世では、新規機能の開発に割く時間を明確に落とすしかありません。あくまで経営者である CTO には取りにくい判断なのは重々承知です（僕もそうなので）。
・「対応AIで」と思うかも知れません。これは技術的には正しいです。ただ、組織的には正しくないです。確実になんとかならず、組織は疲弊していきます。
・なんせセキュリティ対応は大抵自分にタイミングが御せないからです。深夜の対応、急な対応、計画の変更、デグレへの不安、脆弱性情報過多（そもそも自社に影響があるかも分からないものが大半なのに）… と、ストレスの強度がぐんぐん高まっていきます。昨日〜今朝のPHP対応のようなものが、毎週あれば、チームは比較的簡単に壊れてしまうでしょう。
・敢えてリーダーが、セキュリティへの、時間・お金（・トークン）にアロケしてください。これは経営者にしか取れない択で、かついま技術経営者に求められることです。

Point 2: 「必要なら予防的にサービス停止」の覚悟を決め、予めできる調整を重ねたい。止められない場合は、仮想パッチ・監視へのリソースアロケを。
・前提、今回のPHPの件のような脆弱性の対応では、「顧客の保護のためならサービスを止めざるを得ない場面」が訪れます。今回も様々なビジネスがそれに直面しました。今後も訪れるでしょう。
・今回の経験を旨に、本当に止めてはならないのか、止めらるのか、止めうる期待値調整がお客様と出来ているか、を徹底的に見直しておきましょう。
・直近の流れをうけての、お客様への事前連絡（スタンス表明）も有効だと思います。（弊社 GMO Flatt Security 製品についても、これからそれをし、リリースノートとして掲示予定です。我々のサービスの侵害、特に Takumi Guard の侵害は、ソフトウェサプライチェーンの最悪な侵害につながるからです。）
・勿論、止めてはならないビジネスも様々存在します。ビジネスドメインに由来する規制/制約（特に金融・医療セグメント）もあれば、顧客とのSLAもあるでしょう。ただし、現代においては、それらに反するリスクと、セキュリティ被害にあうリスクを天秤にかける必要がでてきています。少し前まではサービス停止でのデメリットは容易に考えられても、セキュリティ侵害など考えにくい、という時代でしたが、今はそうではありません。この天秤を再考する必要があります。（なお、「もう何がなんでも止めてはならない」ビジネスは、相当に限定的だと思います。）
・どうしても止めてはならない（もう何がなんでも止めてはならないもの。限定的であれ存在。人命に関わるもの中心）という場合、厳しい戦いになりますが、WAFレイヤなどで緩和策を施しては祈り、監視する、という流れになります。必要なコンポーネント（WAFなど）と運用リソースがあるならば、苦しい時代ですが、休息うまく取りながらやっていきましょう。なければ、これもしんどいですが、整えましょう。

Point 3: もし平時があれば、システムのモダナイズ（Rebuild and Retire）を検討されたい。
・もし自社での緊急対応が落ち着いているならば、レガシーコンポーネント（数年塩漬けのシステム）、誰がメンテできるのか分からないオーパーツ的存在から順に、作り直し（Rebuild）と旧システムの廃止（Retire）を試みてください。新規開発の代わりに、ここにリソースを充てることが CTO/CISO の仕事です。（他の誰もそれを決められないので。）これは追々自分たちを助けてくれる（ついでにAI-native 開発に移行できて改善しやすくなる）とも思料。
・どのシステムからモダナイズしていくかですが：「XXXで書かれているとまずい」というのは燃えるし言いにくいものの、memory unsafe な言語、type safety があまり確保されていない言語の実装は、モダナイズを検討すべきでしょう。（僕はPHP好きですが、C/C++ で書かれた php-src は、やはりメモリバグ類に対して見通しに限界がありますね。好きなんですが…）
・また経験上、開発当時に DevOps プラクティスすら整っていなかった時代のソフトウェアも、モダナイズを検討したほうがよいです。「セキュリティ診断」をしても、取り返しのつかない量の脆弱性が出てきて、作り直したほうが早い、となる傾向にあります。（弊社でも診断/ペネトレしてますが、こうなると、どうしようもありません。）
・ただし Rebuild には、強いソフトウェア開発力が必要で、AI-native なスタイルに移行することは必須です。この意味で CTO の力がいります。かつ、どこからレガシーの追い出しをするか、どうレキュリティ的なレジリエンスを確保するかは、CISO 的な感性が求められます。既製品（とくに SaaS）を買って処理したほうがいいな、というような判断には CIO 的センスが求められます。総力戦だと思ってください。

Point 4: CTO/CISO の総力戦を。
・Point 3でも述べた通り、直近のくだりには、CTO/CISO の総力戦が必要です。ボードがセキュリティに向かって一致団結する必要があります。
・結構これらロールの間にサイロがあるケースがありますが、そんなことを言っている場合ではありません。
・団結を！
You can read the full English transcript of the podcast episode with @yukihiro_matz #rebuildfm

The China state-aligned threat actor Storm-0940 used the agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate attacks targeting hundreds of organizations globally across a broad range of industries. Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that Storm-0940 was responsible for the recently disclosed ConnectWise supply chain compromise of a multitenant application. https://t.co/VXovj0jI90

Our investigation found that Storm-0940's use of ARTEX accelerated the speed of compromised application abuse to authenticate to target environments through applications that had already been granted access, allowing the threat actor to operate without requiring an interactive user sign-in. AI-accelerated follow-on activity included reconnaissance, application credential changes, and attempts to modify privileges that could enable expanded or persistent access.

Read our blog for a detailed analysis and indicators of compromise (IOCs), along with Microsoft Defender detections, protection recommendations, and guidance on investigating service principal sign-ins and unexpected application credential or privilege changes.

What a day…

The future of cybersecurity is swarms. Swarms of agents attacking and swarms of agents defending.

Or rather, fleets vs. swarms: Governed agents on defense, vs cheap and relentless agents on offense.

Whoever coordinates faster wins.
